province-of-south-australia.t: Australia's planned free colony, founded on Wakefield's theories of systematic settlement and later a pioneer of democratic reforms.
province-of-south-australia.o: Inspired by [[e:edward-gibbon-wakefield|Edward Gibbon Wakefield's]] ideas, the [[e:south-australian-colonisation-commission|South Australian Colonisation Commission]] sold land to fund free emigration, so that the new colony would receive no convicts. The first settlers arrived in 1836 and Governor [[e:john-hindmarsh|John Hindmarsh]] proclaimed the province at [[e:holdfast-bay|Holdfast Bay]] on 28 December. [[e:william-light|Colonel William Light]] chose and laid out the site of [[e:adelaide|Adelaide]].
province-of-south-australia.r: Early financial crisis forced Governor [[e:george-grey|George Grey]] to impose austerity in the 1840s, but [[e:copper|copper]] finds at [[e:kapunda|Kapunda]] and [[e:burra-south-australia|Burra]] and wheat farming brought prosperity. Many Lutheran settlers came from [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and religious dissenters gave the colony a reputation for tolerance. It introduced the secret ballot and adult male suffrage in 1856, the [[e:torrens-title|Torrens title]] system of land registration in 1858, and votes for women in 1894.
province-of-south-australia.e: South [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] also administered the Northern Territory from 1863 to 1911, building the Overland [[e:telegraph|Telegraph]] from Adelaide to [[e:darwin-northern-territory|Darwin]] in 1872. It joined the federation and became a state of the Commonwealth of [[e:australia|Australia]] in 1901.

pan-pan.t: A small Indianised kingdom on the Malay Peninsula that sent envoys to China in the 5th to 7th centuries and was known for its Brahmins and Buddhist monks.
pan-pan.o: Pan Pan appears in Chinese dynastic histories from 424, when it began sending tribute missions to the [[s:liu-song|Liu Song]] court. Its location is uncertain: most scholars place it on the east coast of the [[e:malay-peninsula|Malay Peninsula]], perhaps around the [[e:bay-of-bandon|Bay of Bandon]] near [[e:surat-thani|Surat Thani]], though [[s:kelantan-sultanate|Kelantan]] and [[s:terengganu-sultanate|Terengganu]] have also been proposed.
pan-pan.r: Chinese sources describe a kingdom where many [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] from [[e:india|India]] lived and were honoured by the king, and where there were Buddhist monasteries and monks who studied the scriptures. Like other peninsular ports, it profited from trade crossing the isthmus between the [[e:bay-of-bengal|Bay of Bengal]] and the [[e:south-china-sea|South China Sea]], offering aromatics and other local goods.
pan-pan.e: Missions from Pan Pan stop being recorded after the 7th century, and it was probably absorbed into larger networks such as [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]] or the states that became [[s:tambralinga|Tambralinga]]. Its main interest today lies in what it shows of early Indian religious influence on the peninsula.

panama-canal-zone.t: Strip of land across Panama governed by the United States for 76 years, where the Panama Canal was built and run.
panama-canal-zone.o: The [[e:hay-bunau-varilla-treaty|Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty]] of November 1903 granted the [[s:united-states|United States]], in perpetuity, rights over a zone about ten miles wide across the isthmus, as if it were sovereign. American construction began in 1904; [[e:william-c-gorgas|William Gorgas]]'s campaign against mosquitoes conquered yellow fever, and [[e:george-washington-goethals|George Washington Goethals]] completed the canal, which opened in August 1914.
panama-canal-zone.r: The zone was run by a governor, who also headed the canal company, and was administered from [[e:balboa-heights|Balboa Heights]]. American civilians, known as [[e:zonians|Zonians]], lived in subsidised towns, while the many West Indian workers were paid on a separate [[e:silver|silver]] roll and lived under segregation. US military bases, including Southern Command, made the zone a strategic hub. Panamanians resented the foreign enclave, and the flag riots of January 1964 left over twenty dead.
panama-canal-zone.e: The [[e:torrijos-carter-treaties|Torrijos-Carter Treaties]] of 1977 abolished the Canal Zone on 1 October 1979, returning most of its territory to the [[s:republic-of-panama|Republic of Panama]]. A joint commission ran the canal until Panama took full control on 31 December 1999.

principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.t: A Catholic line of the counts of Oettingen in the Ries, which inherited much of the family's lands in 1731 and became princely in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]] ruled the [[e:nordlinger-ries|Ries crater]] basin from the 12th century. In 1522 the house split into the Oettingen-Oettingen line, which became Lutheran, and the Catholic [[s:principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein|Oettingen-Wallerstein]] line. A Catholic branch formed at Spielberg in the 17th century inherited much of the Oettingen-Oettingen lands in 1731 and received princely rank in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.r: The princes ruled from [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]], a town long divided along its main street between Catholic and Lutheran halves, a legacy of the dynasty's split. The territory lived from farming in the fertile [[e:nordlinger-ries|Ries]] and belonged to the [[e:swabian-circle|Swabian Circle]].
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.e: In 1806 the principality was mediatised and placed under the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. The princely family of Oettingen-Spielberg still owns the residence palace at [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]] in [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Bayern]].

proto-kingdom-of-thinis.t: The kingdom of Thinis and Abydos, whose Dynasty 0 rulers left the earliest Egyptian writing and went on to unite Egypt.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.o: [[e:thinis|Thinis]], near [[s:abydos|Abydos]] in [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]], became the seat of a line of rulers in the late 4th millennium BCE. Their burials in Cemetery U at Abydos grew steadily richer, and by c. 3200 BCE the Thinite chiefs had absorbed the [[s:proto-kingdom-of-naqada|Proto-kingdom of Naqada]] and extended their reach over the [[s:proto-kingdom-of-nekhen|Proto-kingdom of Nekhen]].
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.r: [[e:tomb-u-j|Tomb U-j]] at [[s:abydos|Abydos]], built around 3320 BCE, contained hundreds of imported Levantine wine jars and small bone labels carrying some of the earliest known Egyptian writing. Kings now wrote their names inside a serekh, a palace façade topped by the [[e:horus|Horus]] falcon. These rulers, known today as Dynasty 0, ran an economy of grain, wine and prestige goods and pushed their trade into the Delta.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.e: The Thinite line culminated in [[e:narmer|Narmer]], who around 3100 BCE ruled both Upper and [[e:lower-egypt|Lower Egypt]] and is usually counted as the founder of [[s:early-dynastic-egypt|Early Dynastic Egypt]]. [[s:abydos|Abydos]] remained the burial ground of the [[e:old-babylonian-empire|First Dynasty]] kings and later became the great cult centre of [[e:osiris|Osiris]].

province-of-canada.t: The British colony that united Upper and Lower Canada in 1841, won responsible government, and ended in deadlock that produced Confederation.
province-of-canada.o: Following the rebellions of 1837 and 1838 and [[e:john-lambton-1st-earl-of-durham|Lord Durham's]] report, the [[e:act-of-union-1840|Act of Union]] of 1840 merged [[s:upper-canada|Upper Canada]] and [[s:lower-canada|Lower Canada]] into a single province, proclaimed in February 1841. The two halves, known as [[s:canada|Canada]] West and [[e:canada-east|Canada East]], received equal seats in the assembly despite [[e:canada|Canada]] East's larger population.
province-of-canada.r: The capital moved between [[e:kingston-ontario|Kingston]], [[e:montreal|Montreal]], [[e:toronto|Toronto]] and [[e:quebec|Quebec City]] until [[e:queen-victoria|Queen Victoria]] chose [[e:ottawa|Ottawa]] in 1857. Reformers [[e:robert-baldwin|Robert Baldwin]] and [[e:louis-hippolyte-lafontaine|Louis-Hippolyte LaFontaine]] achieved responsible government in 1848, confirmed when [[e:james-bruce-8th-earl-of-elgin|Lord Elgin]] signed the [[e:rebellion-losses-bill|Rebellion Losses Bill]] despite riots that burned Montreal's parliament in 1849. Canals, the [[e:grand-trunk-railway|Grand Trunk Railway]] and the [[e:canadian-american-reciprocity-treaty|Reciprocity Treaty]] of 1854 with the [[s:united-states|United States]] boosted trade.
province-of-canada.e: By the 1860s sectional rivalry made stable government impossible. [[e:john-a-macdonald|John A. Macdonald]], [[e:george-etienne-cartier|George-Étienne Cartier]] and [[e:george-brown-canadian-politician|George Brown]] formed the Great Coalition of 1864 to pursue federation, and in 1867 the province was split into [[e:ontario|Ontario]] and [[s:province-of-quebec|Quebec]] within the new [[s:canada|Canada]].

principality-of-grubenhagen.t: Small Guelph principality in the western Harz and around Einbeck, famous for its beer, whose line died out in 1596.
principality-of-grubenhagen.o: When the sons of Albert I of [[e:brunswick|Brunswick]] divided their inheritance around 1291, Henry I the Admirable received Grubenhagen, named after a castle near [[e:einbeck|Einbeck]], with lands in the western [[e:harz|Harz]] around [[e:osterode-am-harz|Osterode]] and [[e:herzberg-am-harz|Herzberg]]. This became a separate [[e:house-of-welf|Guelph]] principality.
principality-of-grubenhagen.r: The principality was small, divided at times among co-rulers. Its towns included [[e:einbeck|Einbeck]], whose beer was exported across northern [[e:europe|Europe]], and [[e:osterode-am-harz|Osterode]]. [[e:silver|Silver]] mining in the [[e:harz|Harz]] around [[e:clausthal-zellerfeld|Clausthal]] brought income. Philip I introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1530s. [[e:herzberg-am-harz|Herzberg]] castle served as the main residence.
principality-of-grubenhagen.e: When Philip II died without heirs in 1596, [[e:henry-julius-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg|Henry Julius]] of the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]] seized Grubenhagen, but in 1617 an imperial court awarded it to the [[s:principality-of-luneburg|Principality of Lüneburg]]. It later formed part of the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] and is now in [[e:lower-saxony|Lower Saxony]].

palenque.t: The Classic Maya kingdom of B'aakal in the Chiapas foothills, whose elegant architecture and the tomb of K'inich Janaab Pakal made it one of the best known Maya cities.
palenque.o: Palenque, anciently Lakamha', lies on a ridge above the Gulf lowlands of [[e:chiapas|Chiapas]]. Its kings counted their dynasty from [[e:kuk-bahlam-i|K'uk' B'ahlam I]], who took power in 431 CE, and the city grew as the seat of the B'aakal kingdom.
palenque.r: Palenque was sacked twice by the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]], in 599 and 611, but recovered under [[e:kinich-janaab-pakal|K'inich Janaab Pakal]], who reigned from 615 to 683. He built the Palace with its tower and the Temple of the Inscriptions, where his tomb with its carved sarcophagus lid was found in 1952. His son [[e:kinich-kan-bahlam-ii|K'inich Kan B'ahlam II]] built the [[e:cross-group|Cross Group]]. Palenque was notable for women rulers, its stucco art and long texts.
palenque.e: [[s:tonina|Toniná]] captured the king [[e:kan-joy-chitam-ii|K'an Joy Chitam II]] in 711, and Palenque declined through the 8th century. The last recorded ruler acceded in 799, and the city was abandoned soon after.

prince-bishopric-of-freising.t: The Bavarian church state of Saint Corbinian, a small principality on the Isar with scattered estates reaching into Austria and Carniola.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.o: The diocese goes back to [[e:corbinian|Saint Corbinian]], who worked at [[e:freising|Freising]] around 720, and was formally organised by [[e:saint-boniface|Saint Boniface]] in 739. Over the following centuries the [[e:bishop|bishops]] gathered estates across [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]], [[e:austria|Austria]], [[e:tyrol|Tyrol]] and [[e:carniola|Carniola]]. Their territory as an imperial principality took shape around the city and the county of Werdenfels, bought in 1294.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.r: The [[e:bishop|bishop]], elected by the cathedral chapter, ruled as a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], but his small core lands were surrounded by [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] and he depended heavily on the [[e:house-of-wittelsbach|Wittelsbach]] dukes, several of whose sons held the see. [[e:freising|Freising's]] cathedral hill was a centre of learning, and the nearby abbey of Weihenstephan brewed beer. The territory remained Catholic.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.e: In 1802 and 1803 the prince-bishopric was secularised and its lands passed to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], while estates in [[e:austria|Austria]] went to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]]. The see moved to [[e:munich|Munich]] in 1821 as the [[e:archdiocese-of-munich-and-freising|Archdiocese of Munich and Freising]].

prince-bishopric-of-minden.t: Weser valley church state founded after Charlemagne's Saxon wars and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.o: The diocese of [[e:minden|Minden]] was founded around 800 after [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] conquest of the [[s:saxons|Saxons]], on a crossing of the [[e:weser|Weser]]. Its [[e:bishop|bishops]] gained counties and immunities from the Ottonian and Salian kings. After [[e:henry-the-lion|Henry the Lion]] fell in 1180 they ruled a territory along the Weser as imperial princes, though Minden itself grew increasingly self-governing.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.r: The cathedral chapter elected the [[e:bishop|bishops]], who often lived at [[e:petershagen|Petershagen]] because of friction with [[e:minden|Minden's]] citizens. Their land was small, rural and hemmed in by neighbours such as the counties of Schaumburg, [[s:county-of-ravensberg|Ravensberg]] and Hoya. The city of Minden adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1530, and in the later 16th century the see was held by Lutheran princes of the houses of Brunswick-[[e:luneburg|Lüneburg]] and Schaumburg.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.e: At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 the see was secularised as the [[s:principality-of-minden|Principality of Minden]] and given to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]]. It remained Prussian, apart from the Napoleonic period, and the town is now in [[e:north-rhine-westphalia|North Rhine-Westphalia]].

plaisance.t: France's fortified fishing colony on the south coast of Newfoundland, which raided English settlements before being ceded to Britain in 1713.
plaisance.o: French fishing crews had long used the sheltered harbour of Plaisance, now Placentia, on the [[e:avalon-peninsula|Avalon Peninsula]]. French claims to the harbour date from the 1650s, but the colony is usually dated from 1662, when a garrison and the first resident governor arrived, making Plaisance the administrative centre of French [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]].
plaisance.r: Plaisance was a small military and fishing post with a few hundred residents and many more seasonal fishermen from [[e:saint-malo|Saint-Malo]] and the Basque coast. Its governors, such as [[e:jacques-francois-de-brouillan|Jacques-François de Brouillan]], oversaw Fort Saint-Louis and the dry cod trade. In 1696 to 1697 [[e:pierre-le-moyne-diberville|Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville]] led raids from Plaisance that destroyed most English settlements on [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]], including [[e:st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador|St John's]].
plaisance.e: By the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 [[e:france|France]] ceded [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]] to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], keeping only fishing rights on part of the coast. Governor [[e:philippe-pastour-de-costebelle|Philippe Pastour de Costebelle]] moved the settlers to [[e:louisbourg|Louisbourg]] on [[s:ile-royale|Ile Royale]], and Placentia became a British garrison town in the [[s:colony-of-newfoundland|Colony of Newfoundland]].

peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.t: The revolutionary state born in Zanzibar's violent overthrow of the sultan in January 1964, which lasted three months before union with Tanganyika.
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.o: A month after the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]] became independent, on 12 January 1964 an uprising led by the Ugandan-born [[e:john-okello|John Okello]] and supporters of the [[e:afro-shirazi-party|Afro-Shirazi Party]] overthrew [[e:jamshid-bin-abdullah|Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah]] and the Arab-dominated government. [[e:abeid-karume|Abeid Karume]] of the Afro-Shirazi Party became president of the People's Republic of Zanzibar and [[e:pemba-island|Pemba]].
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.r: The revolution was accompanied by mass killings of [[e:arabs|Arabs]] and South Asians, with thousands dead, and the confiscation of property. A Revolutionary Council ruled by decree, and the new state turned to the Soviet bloc, [[e:china|China]] and [[e:east-germany|East Germany]] for support, raising Western fears of an African [[e:cuba|Cuba]].
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.e: On 26 April 1964 [[e:abeid-karume|Karume]] and [[e:julius-nyerere|Julius Nyerere]] joined [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] with [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] to form the [[e:united-republic-of-tanganyika-and-zanzibar|United Republic]], later named [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]]. Zanzibar kept its own president and government within the union.

principality-of-bzhedugh.t: A princely Circassian tribe on the lower Kuban, one of the few Adyghe groups that largely remained in their homeland after 1864.
principality-of-bzhedugh.o: The Bzhedugh were one of the aristocratic [[e:circassians|Adyghe]] tribes of [[s:circassia|Circassia]], living along the left bank of the Kuban and the [[e:psekups|Psekups]] river near modern [[e:krasnodar|Krasnodar]]. They are recorded as a distinct princely community by the 16th and 17th centuries; their earlier history is not recorded separately.
principality-of-bzhedugh.r: Princes and nobles held power over free peasants and serfs. When the commoners of the [[s:shapsugs|Shapsugs]] and [[s:natukhaj|Natukhaj]] rebelled against their nobility, Bzhedugh princes backed the aristocrats and were defeated at [[e:battle-of-bziyuqo|Bziyuqo]] in 1796. The tribe lay close to Russian forts on the Kuban and often negotiated with [[e:russia|Russia]] while trading and fighting with it.
principality-of-bzhedugh.e: The Bzhedugh came under Russian control in the course of the [[e:russo-circassian-war|Russo-Circassian War]], which the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] completed in 1864. More of them stayed than most Circassian groups, and they form a large part of the [[e:circassians|Adyghe]] population of [[e:adygea|Adygea]] today.

pakao.t: Mandinka district of the middle Casamance known as a centre of Muslim scholarship in a largely non-Muslim region.
pakao.o: Known mainly from oral tradition and colonial records. Pakao was settled by [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] families along the north bank of the [[e:casamance|Casamance]] river, probably by the 16th century, at the edge of the [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu Empire's]] sphere.
pakao.r: Pakao was organised as a set of villages under chiefs, but stood out for its clerical lineages, who ran Quranic schools and spread [[e:islam|Islam]] among neighbouring peoples. It paid tribute to [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]] and maintained ties with Gambian [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] states.
pakao.e: In the second half of the 19th century Pakao was caught up in the wars of [[e:fula|Fula]] and [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] Muslim leaders and then came under French rule, becoming part of [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]] by the 1880s.

provisional-government-of-hawaii.t: The government set up by American and European businessmen after the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, created to secure annexation by the United States.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.o: In January 1893 Queen Liliʻuokalani proposed a new constitution to restore royal power. A [[e:committee-of-safety-hawaii|Committee of Safety]] led by [[e:lorrin-a-thurston|Lorrin A. Thurston]], made up mostly of American [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] interests, seized government buildings on 17 January, while the US minister [[e:john-l-stevens|John L. Stevens]] landed marines from USS [[e:boston|Boston]]. The queen yielded under protest to the superior force of the [[s:united-states|United States]], and the committee proclaimed a provisional government.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.r: [[e:sanford-b-dole|Sanford B. Dole]] headed an executive council, with an advisory council of the overthrow's supporters, and ruled without elections, requiring officials to swear loyalty. Its single goal was annexation, and it quickly sent a treaty to [[e:washington-dc|Washington]]. It kept the [[s:kingdom-of-hawaii|Kingdom of Hawaii]]'s laws and bureaucracy largely in place.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.e: President [[e:grover-cleveland|Grover Cleveland]] withdrew the treaty and, after the [[e:blount-report|Blount Report]] found American complicity, asked for the queen's restoration. [[e:sanford-b-dole|Dole]] refused. To secure itself until annexation became possible, the government proclaimed the [[s:republic-of-hawaii|Republic of Hawaii]] on 4 July 1894. The [[s:united-states|United States]] formally apologised for the overthrow in 1993.

cr.a: FOTW, Clay Moss (PNG), Government of the Republic of Hawaii

paeligni.t: Sabellic people of the Abruzzo mountains whose town Corfinium became the rebel capital of the Social War and whose Sulmo was Ovid's birthplace.
paeligni.o: The Paeligni lived in the upland basin of the [[e:aterno-pescara|Aterno]] and Gizio rivers in central [[e:abruzzo|Abruzzo]], surrounded by the [[s:marsi|Marsi]], [[s:vestini|Vestini]] and [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]], from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples descended from the [[s:sabines|Sabines]], and they spoke a dialect close to [[e:oscan-language|Oscan]].
paeligni.r: Their main towns were [[e:corfinium|Corfinium]], [[e:sulmona|Sulmo]] and Superaequum, small hill communities that formed a league. Inscriptions in the Paelignian dialect, many in [[e:latin|Latin]] letters, record local gods and priestesses. They kept sheep and controlled routes through the [[e:apennines|Apennines]] between [[e:rome|Rome]] and the Adriatic.
paeligni.e: The Paeligni made peace and an alliance with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 304 BCE, together with the [[s:marsi|Marsi]] and [[s:marrucini|Marrucini]]. In 91 BCE they joined the Italian revolt, and [[e:corfinium|Corfinium]] was renamed [[s:italia-social-war-confederation|Italia]] as the capital of the rebel confederation. After the Social War they received citizenship; the poet [[e:ovid|Ovid]] was born at [[e:sulmona|Sulmo]] in 43 BCE.

patriarchate-of-aquileia.t: A church principality in Friuli whose patriarchs ruled as imperial princes for over three centuries and whose parliament was among Europe's earliest.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.o: During the Investiture Controversy, [[e:henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Henry IV]] rewarded Patriarch [[e:sigehard-of-aquileia|Sigehard of Aquileia]] for his loyalty by granting him the county of [[e:friuli|Friuli]] in 1077, soon followed by [[s:histria|Istria]] and [[e:carniola|Carniola]]. The patriarchs thus became temporal princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], heirs to one of the oldest bishoprics in the [[e:latin|Latin]] West.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.r: Patriarchs, usually German nobles in the early centuries and later Italians or Frenchmen, ruled from [[e:aquileia|Aquileia]], [[e:cividale-del-friuli|Cividale]] and from the 13th century mainly [[e:udine|Udine]]. The [[e:parliament-of-friuli|Parliament of Friuli]], bringing together clergy, nobles and towns, voted taxes and troops. The principality was constantly squeezed by the counts of [[e:gorizia|Gorizia]], the [[s:duchy-of-austria|Duchy of Austria]] and the [[s:republic-of-venice|Republic of Venice]]; [[e:bertrand-of-saint-genies|Patriarch Bertrand]] was murdered by Friulian nobles in 1350.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.e: [[e:venice|Venice]] conquered [[e:friuli|Friuli]] in 1420, ending the patriarchs' temporal rule; a settlement in 1445 left them only a few towns. The patriarchate continued as a church office until 1751, when Pope [[e:benedict-xiv|Benedict XIV]] divided it into the archdioceses of [[e:udine|Udine]] and [[e:gorizia|Gorizia]].

picentes.t: Italic people of the central Adriatic coast, said to have followed a woodpecker to their new land, whose warrior culture lasted until Rome conquered them in 268 BCE.
picentes.o: The Picentes lived in [[e:picenum|Picenum]], the coastal strip and hills of the modern [[e:marche|Marche]] and northern [[e:abruzzo|Abruzzo]], from the early 1st millennium BCE. Roman tradition said they descended from [[s:sabines|Sabines]] who left home in a 'sacred spring' migration, guided by a woodpecker (picus), the bird of [[e:mars-mythology|Mars]]. Archaeologists call their culture the Picene culture.
picentes.r: Picene society was dominated by warrior elites buried with helmets, weapons, [[e:chariot|chariots]] and amber from the Baltic. Their [[e:south-picene-language|South Picene]] inscriptions, in a Sabellic language written in a distinctive alphabet, appear on stone stelae, and the [[e:novilara-stele|Novilara stele]] in the north bears a still undeciphered text. [[e:ascoli-piceno|Asculum]] was their main centre, and they traded across the Adriatic and with [[e:etruria|Etruria]].
picentes.e: The Picentes allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 299 BCE but revolted in 269 BCE and were conquered in 268 BCE; part of the population was moved to the [[e:gulf-of-salerno|Gulf of Salerno]]. [[e:ascoli-piceno|Asculum]] became an allied city, and its massacre of [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] in 91 BCE began the [[e:social-war-91-87-bce|Social War]]. [[e:picenum|Picenum]] became part of Augustus's Regio V.

cr.a: Dbachmann; derivative work by Ewan ar born translator: Manlleus (ca)

pacajes.t: An Aymara kingdom on the southern shore of Lake Titicaca whose territory included Tiwanaku and later became a key Spanish province.
pacajes.o: The Pacajes, or Pakasa, formed one of the [[e:aymara|Aymara]] kingdoms that emerged around [[e:lake-titicaca|Lake Titicaca]] after Tiwanaku's collapse, occupying the high plain south of the lake in modern [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]] from the 12th century. Their capital was Caquiaviri.
pacajes.r: Like other [[e:aymara|Aymara]] kingdoms, Pacajes was divided into two halves, Urcosuyu and Umasuyu, each with its own lords. Its economy was based on herding llamas and alpacas and farming tubers such as [[e:potato|potatoes]], freeze-dried into chuño. Pacajes lords built chullpa burial towers and kept colonies in warmer valleys to the east.
pacajes.e: Pacajes was absorbed into the [[s:inca-empire|Inca Empire]] in the mid-15th century. Under Spanish rule it became a province of the [[s:royal-audiencia-of-charcas|Royal Audiencia of Charcas]], and its people supplied labour for the [[e:potosi|Potosí]] mines under the [[e:mita|mita]]. Caquiaviri retains a notable colonial church.

prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.t: Alpine church state that grew rich on salt and gold, built a baroque capital, expelled its Protestants in 1731 and employed the young Mozart.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.o: [[e:rupert-of-salzburg|Saint Rupert]] founded a church and monastery at the Roman town of [[e:iuvavum|Iuvavum]] around 696, and [[e:salzburg|Salzburg]] became an archbishopric in 798. Its archbishops gained lands and immunities over the centuries, and by the early 13th century, around 1213, they were recognised as princes ruling a territory largely independent of the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Duchy of Bavaria]].
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.r: The archbishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, governed a land whose wealth came from salt at [[e:hallein|Hallein]] and gold and [[e:silver|silver]] mines in the [[e:gastein-valley|Gastein]] valley. [[e:wolf-dietrich-von-raitenau|Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau]] and [[e:markus-sittikus-von-hohenems|Markus Sittikus]] rebuilt [[e:salzburg|Salzburg]] in Italian baroque style, and [[e:paris-lodron|Paris Lodron]] kept it out of the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]]. In 1731 [[e:leopold-anton-von-firmian|Leopold Anton von Firmian]] expelled about 20,000 Protestants. [[e:wolfgang-amadeus-mozart|Mozart]] was born there in 1756 and served Archbishop [[e:hieronymus-von-colloredo|Hieronymus von Colloredo]].
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.e: The see was secularised in 1803 as the [[s:electorate-of-salzburg|Electorate of Salzburg]] for [[e:ferdinand-iii-grand-duke-of-tuscany|Ferdinand of Tuscany]], then passed to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1805 and to [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] in 1810. In 1816 most of it was returned to Austria, of which it is now a federal state.

cr.a: Roke (map), Hanno Sandvik (addition of colours, based on Putzger Historischer Weltatlas, 103rd ed., 2005)

prince-bishopric-of-liege.t: A church principality on the Meuse that lasted eight centuries, grew rich on coal and arms making, and balanced its bishops against assertive townspeople.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.o: [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:notger|Notger]] (972–1008) gathered secular rights from the Ottonian emperors, including the county of Huy in 985, and turned the see of Liège into a territorial principality of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]]. He rebuilt the city and its schools, and Liège became one of the leading intellectual centres of the empire.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] shared power with the cathedral chapter and towns; the [[e:peace-of-fexhe|Peace of Fexhe]] of 1316 required the consent of the estates for major decisions. Liège mined [[e:coal|coal]] from the 12th century and became famous for metalwork and weapons. [[e:charles-the-bold|Charles the Bold]] sacked the city in 1468. [[e:erard-de-la-marck|Erard de la Marck]] rebuilt it in the early 16th century, and the principality kept a careful neutrality.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.e: The [[s:republic-of-liege|Liège Revolution]] of 1789 drove out the prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]] and created the Republic of Liège; Austrian troops restored him in 1791. French armies annexed the principality in 1795, and its lands were later divided between [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]].

principality-of-salm.t: A Vosges principality of the Salm family around the abbey town of Senones, which voted to join France in 1793.
principality-of-salm.o: The counts of Salm, a branch of the Wild- and Rhinegraves, held lands in the [[e:vosges|Vosges]] around [[s:senones|Senones]] and Badonviller. In 1623 [[e:philip-otto-of-salm|Philip Otto of Salm]] was made a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], and the territory became a principality.
principality-of-salm.r: The principality was a small mountain land of forests, ironworks and later textile workshops. Its life centred on [[s:senones|Senones]] and its Benedictine abbey, whose abbot [[e:augustin-calmet|Dom Augustin Calmet]] was a celebrated scholar. In 1751 the territory was reorganised and Senones became the princes' residence, with a modest court.
principality-of-salm.e: Surrounded by [[e:french-first-republic|Revolutionary France]] and cut off by its [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]], the inhabitants voted to join [[e:france|France]], and the [[s:french-first-republic|French First Republic]] annexed the principality in 1793. The [[s:principality-of-salm-1802|Salm-Salm]] princes received compensation in [[e:westphalia|Westphalia]].

pahra-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs near Kalinjar in Bundelkhand, created by the British in 1812.
pahra-state.o: Pahra was one of the estates granted in 1812 to members of the Chaube family, [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] governors of [[e:kalinjar-fort|Kalinjar]] fort, when they surrendered the fortress to the British.
pahra-state.r: It was a minor holding of a few villages under the [[e:bundelkhand-agency|Bundelkhand Agency]]. Little else is recorded.
pahra-state.e: After independence Pahra was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

panna-state.t: The Bundela kingdom of Chhatrasal in Bundelkhand, famous for its diamond mines and as a holy centre of the Pranami faith.
panna-state.o: [[e:chhatrasal|Chhatrasal]], a [[e:bundelas|Bundela]] [[e:rajputs|Rajput]], rebelled against Mughal rule from the 1670s and built an independent kingdom with its capital at Panna. With [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] help under [[e:baji-rao-i|Baji Rao I]] he defeated a Mughal invasion in 1729; on his death his realm was divided among his heirs and the [[e:peshwa|Peshwa]].
panna-state.r: The [[e:maharaja|Maharajas]] of Panna ruled the eastern share of [[e:chhatrasal|Chhatrasal's]] kingdom. The state was known for its diamond mines, which gave it revenue for centuries. Chhatrasal's guru [[e:mahamati-prannath|Prannath]] made Panna a sacred centre of the Pranami sect. Under British paramountcy it was a salute state of the [[e:bundelkhand-agency|Bundelkhand Agency]].
panna-state.e: Panna joined [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] in 1948 and [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956. The diamond mines at [[e:majhgawan-diamond-mine|Majhgawan]] and [[e:panna-national-park|Panna National Park]] lie in its former territory.

pellendones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Douro around the Picos de Urbión, living in the high country north of Numantia.
pellendones.o: The Pellendones lived around the sources of the [[e:douro|Douro]] in northern [[e:soria|Soria]] and southern [[e:la-rioja-spain|La Rioja]] from about the 4th century BCE. Pliny counts them among the [[s:celtiberians|Celtiberians]], and some ancient geographers placed [[e:numantia|Numantia]] in their territory rather than that of the [[s:arevaci|Arevaci]].
pellendones.r: They were a highland people of hillforts and herding, with towns such as Visontium and Augustobriga named by Ptolemy. Their society was probably organised in clans under local elites like that of their Celtiberian neighbours, but no details are recorded.
pellendones.e: They were drawn into the Celtiberian wars against [[e:rome|Rome]] and came under Roman control after the fall of [[e:numantia|Numantia]] in 133 BCE, becoming part of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]].

province-of-new-jersey.t: The English colony between the Hudson and Delaware rivers, granted in 1664, split in two for a generation and reunited under the Crown in 1702.
province-of-new-jersey.o: After seizing [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] in 1664, [[e:james-ii-of-england|James, Duke of York]], granted the land between the [[e:hudson-river|Hudson]] and [[e:delaware-river|Delaware]] to Lord [[e:john-berkeley-1st-baron-berkeley-of-stratton|John Berkeley]] and [[e:george-carteret|Sir George Carteret]], naming it after Carteret's home island of [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]]. Their Concession and Agreement of 1665 promised religious freedom and an elected assembly, drawing settlers to [[e:elizabeth-new-jersey|Elizabethtown]] and other towns.
province-of-new-jersey.r: Disputes over land and quitrents led to division into [[s:east-jersey|East Jersey]] and [[s:west-jersey|West Jersey]], which existed from 1674 until the proprietors surrendered government to the Crown in 1702. The reunited royal colony shared its governor with the [[s:province-of-new-york|Province of New York]] until 1738, and its capital alternated between [[e:perth-amboy|Perth Amboy]] and [[e:burlington-new-jersey|Burlington]]. Diverse Puritan, [[e:quakers|Quaker]], [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Scottish settlers farmed grain, and the colleges that became [[e:princeton-university|Princeton]] and [[e:rutgers-university|Rutgers]] were founded in 1746 and 1766.
province-of-new-jersey.e: Royal governor [[e:william-franklin|William Franklin]], son of [[e:benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]], was arrested in 1776. On 2 July 1776 [[e:new-jersey|New Jersey]] adopted a state constitution, and it became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

cr.a: AnonMoos, based on image by Zscout370, AnonMoos

panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.t: A dynasty of Chhattisgarh ruling from Sirpur, whose brick Lakshmana temple and Buddhist monasteries are among the treasures of early medieval India.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.o: The Panduvamshis, claiming descent from the lunar line, rose in [[e:dakshina-kosala|Dakshina Kosala]], the upper [[e:mahanadi|Mahanadi]] valley of modern [[e:chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]], in the 6th century. Under [[e:tivaradeva|Tivaradeva]] they united the region and made [[e:sirpur-chhattisgarh|Shripura]], modern Sirpur, their capital, displacing earlier local rulers.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.r: The kings were mostly [[e:vaishnavism|Vaishnava]] but tolerant of [[e:shaivism|Shaivism]] and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]]. [[e:mahashivagupta-balarjuna|Mahashivagupta Balarjuna]], who ruled for about sixty years in the 7th century, was a Shaiva who also endowed Buddhist monasteries; his mother Vasata built the [[e:lakshmana-temple-sirpur|Lakshmana temple]] at [[e:sirpur-chhattisgarh|Sirpur]], one of the finest early brick temples in [[e:india|India]]. Excavations at Sirpur have revealed monasteries, markets and temples of a thriving city, which [[e:xuanzang|Xuanzang]] described.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.e: After [[e:mahashivagupta-balarjuna|Balarjuna]] the dynasty declined in the 8th century. Its line, known as the Somavamshis, moved east into [[e:odisha|Odisha]], where it later ruled as the [[s:somavamshi-dynasty|Somavamshi dynasty]], while [[e:dakshina-kosala|Dakshina Kosala]] passed to other rulers.

principality-of-anhalt-dessau.t: The leading Anhalt principality, famed for the Old Dessauer's drill reforms and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm of the Enlightenment.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.o: Anhalt-[[e:dessau|Dessau]] was created in the 1603 partition of [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]], with Prince [[e:john-george-i-prince-of-anhalt-dessau|John George I]] receiving Dessau on the [[e:mulde|Mulde]] near its junction with the [[e:elbe|Elbe]]. The line was Calvinist and closely tied to the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Electorate of Brandenburg]] by marriage.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.r: [[e:leopold-i-prince-of-anhalt-dessau|Leopold I]], the Old Dessauer, was a Prussian field marshal who introduced the iron ramrod and cadenced marching. His grandson [[e:leopold-iii-frederick-franz|Leopold III Friedrich Franz]] was a model [[e:age-of-enlightenment|Enlightenment]] ruler who laid out the landscape gardens of [[e:dessau-worlitz-garden-realm|Wörlitz]], built schools and founded the [[e:philanthropinum|Philanthropinum]], a progressive school, in 1774. The principality became a duchy in 1807.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.e: Anhalt-[[e:dessau|Dessau]] inherited [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]] in 1847 and [[s:principality-of-anhalt-bernburg|Anhalt-Bernburg]] in 1863, after which Duke [[e:leopold-iv-duke-of-anhalt|Leopold IV Friedrich]] ruled a united [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] from Dessau. The Garden Realm is now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

principality-of-orange.t: A tiny sovereign principality in the Rhône valley whose title passed to the house of Nassau and gave the Dutch royal family its name.
principality-of-orange.o: Orange was a Roman colony and later a county within the [[s:kingdom-of-arles|Kingdom of Arles]]; the troubadour [[e:raimbaut-d-orange|Raimbaut d'Orange]] ruled part of it in the 12th century. In 1163 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Emperor Frederick Barbarossa]] raised it to a principality, and it passed in 1173 to [[e:bertrand-of-baux|Bertrand of Baux]], whose family ruled it for over two centuries.
principality-of-orange.r: The principality was a small enclave inside [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] and the [[s:comtat-venaissin|Comtat Venaissin]], with Roman monuments, a university founded in 1365 and its own courts. It passed to the Chalon family in 1393. [[e:rene-of-chalon|René of Chalon]] left it to his cousin William of [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] in 1544, and under [[e:william-the-silent|William the Silent]] Orange became a refuge for Protestants.
principality-of-orange.e: [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] occupied Orange several times and destroyed its fortifications. After the death of [[e:william-iii-of-england|William III of England]] in 1702, [[e:france|France]] took it, and the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 recognised its annexation. The princes of [[e:house-of-orange-nassau|Orange-Nassau]] kept the title, which the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] royal house still bears.

pataudi-state.t: A small Pathan Nawabi state near Delhi, famous in the 20th century for its two cricket-captain Nawabs.
pataudi-state.o: [[e:faiz-talab-khan|Faiz Talab Khan]], a Pathan of the Barech tribe, served the British in the war against the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]], and in 1804 the British granted him the district of Pataudi south-west of [[e:delhi|Delhi]] as a hereditary state.
pataudi-state.r: Pataudi was a small, non-salute state of the [[e:punjab|Punjab]], ruled by a Nawab over a mainly [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] farming population. Nawab [[e:iftikhar-ali-khan-pataudi|Iftikhar Ali Khan Pataudi]] played Test cricket for [[e:england|England]] and later captained [[e:india|India]], and his son [[e:mansoor-ali-khan-pataudi|Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi]] became India's youngest Test captain.
pataudi-state.e: Pataudi acceded to [[e:india|India]] and in 1948 was merged into [[e:east-punjab|East Punjab]]; the town is now in [[e:gurugram|Gurugram]] district of [[e:haryana|Haryana]]. The family's title was abolished with all princely privileges in 1971.

principality-of-blankenburg.t: Harz principality of a Brunswick prince whose daughter became mother of Empress Maria Theresa.
principality-of-blankenburg.o: The County of Blankenburg in the [[e:harz|Harz]] had passed to the dukes of [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel]] in 1599. Duke [[e:anthony-ulrich-duke-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel|Anthony Ulrich]] gave it to his younger son [[e:louis-rudolph-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg|Louis Rudolph]], and in 1707 [[e:joseph-i-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Joseph I]] raised it to a principality, giving Louis Rudolph a seat among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-blankenburg.r: [[e:louis-rudolph-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg|Louis Rudolph]] ruled the small Lutheran territory from Blankenburg Castle, which he rebuilt, with a court [[e:theatre|theatre]] and gardens. The principality's prestige came from [[e:diplomatic-marriage|dynastic marriages]]: his daughter [[e:elisabeth-christine-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel|Elisabeth Christine]] married the future [[e:charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles VI]] and became mother of [[e:maria-theresa|Maria Theresa]], while another daughter married the son of [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great]].
principality-of-blankenburg.e: In 1731 [[e:louis-rudolph-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg|Louis Rudolph]] inherited the Principality of [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel]], and Blankenburg was reunited with it. It remained a [[e:brunswick|Brunswick]] possession and became part of the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick|Duchy of Brunswick]].

cr.a: Gustav Droysen; derivative work by Beckstet

portuguese-angola.t: Portugal's West African colony centred on Luanda, for three centuries the largest source of enslaved Africans shipped to Brazil.
portuguese-angola.o: In 1575 [[e:paulo-dias-de-novais|Paulo Dias de Novais]] arrived on the coast with a royal charter to conquer the [[s:kingdom-of-ndongo|Kingdom of Ndongo]], founding [[e:luanda|Luanda]] the following year. The colony grew from a coastal base through wars with Ndongo, alliances with [[e:imbangala|Imbangala]] bands and the founding of [[e:benguela|Benguela]] in 1617, always driven by the demand for slaves in [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]].
portuguese-angola.r: Governors in [[e:luanda|Luanda]] relied on forts along the [[e:kwanza-river|Kwanza]], African auxiliaries and trading fairs to obtain captives, and Luanda's merchants were closely tied to [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]]. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] occupied Luanda from 1641 until [[e:salvador-correia-de-sa-e-benevides|Salvador Correia de Sa]] recaptured it in 1648. After the end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] in the 19th century, Portugal pushed inland, and 20th-century settlers developed [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], diamonds and later oil.
portuguese-angola.e: Nationalist revolt began in 1961, with the [[e:mpla|MPLA]], [[e:national-liberation-front-of-angola|FNLA]] and [[e:unita|UNITA]] fighting Portugal. After the [[e:carnation-revolution|Carnation Revolution]] of 1974, Portugal withdrew, and [[e:angola|Angola]] became independent on 11 November 1975 amid a civil war between the movements.

peucetians.t: Iapygian people of central Apulia around modern Bari, whose towns such as Rubi became centres of Greek-influenced art and vase collecting.
peucetians.o: The Peucetians occupied central [[e:apulia|Apulia]] between the [[s:daunians|Daunians]] to the north and the [[s:messapians|Messapians]] to the south, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek writers explained their name through [[e:peucetius|Peucetius]], a son of the Arcadian [[e:lycaon-of-arcadia|Lycaon]], but their culture developed from local [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] communities related to their Iapygian neighbours.
peucetians.r: They lived in separate fortified towns, among them Caelia, Azetium, [[e:ruvo-di-puglia|Rubi]] (Ruvo di [[e:apulia|Puglia]]) and the site of [[e:monte-sannace|Monte Sannace]], without a known central government. Their geometric painted pottery gave way, from the 5th century BCE, to strong Greek influence: the elite of Rubi buried their dead with Athenian and Apulian red-figure vases, many from [[s:taras|Taras]]. They grew cereals and olives and traded through coastal landings.
peucetians.e: The Peucetian towns came under Roman control around the end of the 4th and start of the 3rd centuries BCE during [[e:rome|Rome's]] expansion into [[e:apulia|Apulia]]. They were later absorbed into Roman Apulia and became municipia. Collections of vases from [[e:ruvo-di-puglia|Ruvo]], such as the [[e:jatta-national-museum|Jatta collection]], preserve much of their material culture.

palatinate-neuburg.t: The 'Young Palatinate' on the Danube, created after the Landshut War, whose dukes inherited Jülich and Berg and then the Palatine electorate.
palatinate-neuburg.o: The [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] arbitration of 1505 that ended the [[e:war-of-the-landshut-succession|War of the Landshut Succession]] created a new principality from parts of the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria-landshut|Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut]] for [[e:otto-henry-elector-palatine|Otto Henry]] and Philip, the young sons of [[e:rupert-of-germany|Rupert of the Palatinate]]. Known as the Young [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]], it had [[e:neuburg-an-der-donau|Neuburg]] on the [[e:danube|Danube]] as its capital.
palatinate-neuburg.r: [[e:otto-henry-elector-palatine|Otto Henry]] introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1542 and rebuilt [[e:neuburg-an-der-donau|Neuburg]] castle in [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] style before becoming [[e:elector-palatine|Elector Palatine]]. [[e:wolfgang-william-count-palatine-of-neuburg|Wolfgang William]] converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] in 1613 to strengthen his claim in the Jülich succession and won Jülich and Berg, ruling from [[e:dusseldorf|Düsseldorf]]. His son [[e:philip-william-elector-palatine|Philip William]] became Elector Palatine in 1685, after which the Neuburg dukes ruled from Düsseldorf, [[e:heidelberg|Heidelberg]] and [[e:mannheim|Mannheim]].
palatinate-neuburg.e: When Elector [[e:charles-iii-philip-elector-palatine|Charles Philip]], the last of the [[e:neuburg-an-der-donau|Neuburg]] line, died in 1742, his lands passed to [[e:charles-theodore-elector-of-bavaria|Charles Theodore]] of [[s:palatinate-sulzbach|Palatinate-Sulzbach]], who in 1777 also inherited [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]]. Neuburg was absorbed into the [[e:house-of-wittelsbach|Wittelsbach]] lands of Bavaria.

principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.t: The Catholic Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns, ruling from Sigmaringen castle on the Danube, which later gave Romania its kings.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.o: When Count Charles I of the [[s:county-of-hohenzollern|County of Hohenzollern]] died in 1576, his lands were divided among his sons. [[e:charles-ii-count-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen|Charles II]] received [[e:sigmaringen|Sigmaringen]] and Veringen on the upper [[e:danube|Danube]], founding the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line, and the counts were raised to princes in 1623.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.r: The princes ruled a small Catholic territory from [[e:sigmaringen|Sigmaringen's]] castle on a rock above the [[e:danube|Danube]], under strong [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] influence since parts of their lands were Austrian fiefs. Thanks partly to Princess [[e:amalie-zephyrine-of-salm-kyrburg|Amalie Zephyrine]], a friend of [[e:josephine-de-beauharnais|Joséphine de Beauharnais]], the principality survived the mediatisation of 1806, joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and even gained territory.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.e: After the revolution of 1848, Prince [[e:charles-anthony-prince-of-hohenzollern|Charles Anthony]] ceded his [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] to his Prussian cousins in 1849, and in 1850 the principality became part of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. His son [[e:carol-i-of-romania|Carol]] became prince and later king of [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], and another son's candidacy for the Spanish throne helped trigger the [[e:franco-prussian-war|Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870.

province-of-carolina.t: The proprietary colony of eight English lords, whose planned feudal constitution by John Locke gave way to a plantation society centred on Charles Town.
province-of-carolina.o: In 1663 [[e:charles-ii-of-england|Charles II]] granted the land between [[e:virginia|Virginia]] and [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] to eight Lords Proprietors, among them [[e:anthony-ashley-cooper-1st-earl-of-shaftesbury|Anthony Ashley Cooper]] and the [[e:edward-hyde-1st-earl-of-clarendon|Earl of Clarendon]]. Settlers from Virginia had already reached the [[e:albemarle-sound|Albemarle Sound]] region in the north, and in 1670 an expedition largely from [[s:barbados|Barbados]] founded [[e:charleston-south-carolina|Charles Town]], which moved to its present site in 1680.
province-of-carolina.r: The Fundamental Constitutions of 1669, drafted by [[e:anthony-ashley-cooper-1st-earl-of-shaftesbury|Ashley Cooper]] and his secretary [[e:john-locke|John Locke]], proposed a hereditary nobility but were never fully applied. Planters from [[s:barbados|Barbados]] brought the slave plantation system, and a large trade in deerskins and in enslaved Native people grew. [[e:rice|Rice]] became the leading crop in the south from the 1690s, while the distant northern settlements had their own deputy governor and assembly.
province-of-carolina.e: The [[e:tuscarora-war|Tuscarora War]] of 1711 exposed the weakness of the divided colony, and in 1712 the proprietors gave the two parts separate governors, creating the [[s:province-of-north-carolina|Province of North Carolina]] and the [[s:province-of-south-carolina|Province of South Carolina]].

paldeo-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs near Kalinjar in Bundelkhand, granted by the British in 1812.
paldeo-state.o: Paldeo was among the small estates given in 1812 to members of the Chaube family, [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] governors of [[e:kalinjar-fort|Kalinjar]] fort, when they surrendered the fort to the British.
paldeo-state.r: It was a minor holding of a few villages under the [[e:bundelkhand-agency|Bundelkhand Agency]]. Few details of its later history are recorded.
paldeo-state.e: After independence Paldeo was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

paratarajas.t: An obscure dynasty of Balochistan, known almost only from its coins, which ruled on the borderlands of Iran and India.
paratarajas.o: The Paratarajas, kings of the Paratas or Paradas, ruled in what is now [[e:balochistan|Balochistan]] from around the 2nd century. They are known mainly from coins with legends in Brahmi and Kharoshthi that name a sequence of kings and their fathers, and they appear to have been connected to the [[s:indo-parthian-kingdom|Indo-Parthian Kingdom]].
paratarajas.r: Their [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] coins show the king's bust on one side and a swastika on the other, with titles that call the ruler Paratarajas. Kings such as Yolamira and [[e:arjuna|Arjuna]] are known only by name. The state probably controlled routes between the [[e:indus|Indus]] valley and south-eastern [[e:iran|Iran]].
paratarajas.e: The Paratarajas likely came under the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] in the 3rd century; the Paikuli inscription of the Sasanian king [[e:narseh|Narseh]] mentions a ruler of the Paradan among his [[e:vassal|vassals]]. Their coinage ends around 300.

province-of-south-carolina.t: The richest colony in British North America, whose rice and indigo plantations around Charles Town depended on an enslaved African majority.
province-of-south-carolina.o: The southern settlements of the [[s:province-of-carolina|Province of Carolina]], centred on [[e:charleston-south-carolina|Charles Town]], received a separate governor in 1712. After the [[e:yamasee-war|Yamasee War]] of 1715 to 1717 nearly destroyed the colony, settlers overthrew proprietary rule in 1719 and asked for royal government, which the Crown formalised in 1729.
province-of-south-carolina.r: [[e:rice|Rice]] grown in tidal swamps, and from the 1740s [[e:indigo|indigo]], developed by [[e:eliza-lucas-pinckney|Eliza Lucas Pinckney]], made the planter elite of the [[e:south-carolina-lowcountry|Lowcountry]] the wealthiest in British America. Enslaved Africans formed the majority of the population, and the [[e:gullah|Gullah]] language and culture took shape on the coastal plantations. The [[e:stono-rebellion|Stono Rebellion]] of 1739 led to harsh new slave laws. [[e:charleston-south-carolina|Charles Town]] was a lively port with [[e:theatre|theatres]], libraries and the deerskin trade with the [[e:cherokee|Cherokee]] and [[e:muscogee|Muscogee]].
province-of-south-carolina.e: The last royal governor, [[e:lord-william-campbell|Lord William Campbell]], fled in 1775. In March 1776 [[e:south-carolina|South Carolina]] adopted its own constitution, and in June its defenders repulsed a British fleet at [[e:battle-of-sullivans-island|Sullivan's Island]]. It became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

principality-of-salerno.t: Lombard principality of southern Italy, home of the famous medical school of Salerno, conquered by Robert Guiscard in 1077.
principality-of-salerno.o: A long civil war in the [[s:duchy-of-benevento|Principality of Benevento]] ended in 849 with a formal partition: [[e:siconulf|Siconulf]] became prince of Salerno, ruling the western half including the coast of [[e:campania|Campania]], [[e:lucania|Lucania]] and parts of [[e:calabria|Calabria]], while [[e:radelchis-i-of-benevento|Radelchis]] kept [[e:benevento|Benevento]].
principality-of-salerno.r: Salerno was a prosperous coastal city with links to [[s:republic-of-amalfi|Amalfi]] and the Byzantine world. The [[e:schola-medica-salernitana|Schola Medica Salernitana]], the first great medical school of medieval [[e:europe|Europe]], flourished there from the 10th century, drawing on Greek, [[e:latin|Latin]] and Arabic learning. Under [[e:guaimar-iv-of-salerno|Guaimar IV]] (1027–1052) the principality reached its height, controlling Amalfi, [[e:sorrento|Sorrento]] and [[s:principality-of-capua|Capua]], and he invested the Norman leaders with [[e:apulia|Apulia]].
principality-of-salerno.e: After [[e:guaimar-iv-of-salerno|Guaimar IV]] was murdered in 1052, Norman power grew rapidly. [[e:robert-guiscard|Robert Guiscard]], who had married [[e:sichelgaita|Sichelgaita]], sister of Prince [[e:gisulf-ii-of-salerno|Gisulf II]], besieged Salerno and took it in 1077, making it his capital. The principality became part of the Norman [[s:duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria|Duchy of Apulia]].

polemonid-pontus.t: Polemonid Pontus, a Roman client kingdom on the Black Sea ruled by Polemon I, his queen Pythodorida and their son.
polemonid-pontus.o: In 37 BCE [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]] made [[e:polemon-i-of-pontus|Polemon]], son of the orator [[e:zeno-of-laodicea|Zeno of Laodicea]], king of part of the former [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]]. Polemon kept his throne after [[e:battle-of-actium|Actium]] by switching to Augustus and was also made king of the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]].
polemonid-pontus.r: The kingdom covered the eastern Pontic coast and inland valleys, including [[s:trapezus|Trapezus]] and [[e:zela|Zela]]. After [[e:polemon-i-of-pontus|Polemon]] was killed c. 8 BCE, his widow [[e:pythodoris|Pythodorida]], a granddaughter of [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]], ruled in her own name for many years. [[e:strabo|Strabo]], a native of the region, praised her government.
polemonid-pontus.e: [[e:caligula|Caligula]] gave the kingdom to her grandson [[e:polemon-ii-of-pontus|Polemon II]] in 38 CE. [[e:nero|Nero]] deposed him in 62 CE and annexed [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]] to the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]].

principality-of-hungary.t: Hungarian state of the Árpád dynasty in the Carpathian basin, from the conquest of 895 to Stephen's coronation as king in 1000.
principality-of-hungary.o: After [[e:pechenegs|Pecheneg]] attacks drove them from [[e:etelkoz|Etelköz]], the [[s:hungarian-tribal-federation|Hungarian tribal federation]] under [[e:arpad|Árpád]] crossed the [[e:carpathian-mountains|Carpathians]] in 895. By the first years of the 10th century they held the whole basin, and in 907 they destroyed a Bavarian army at [[e:bratislava|Pressburg]], securing the conquest.
principality-of-hungary.r: For half a century Hungarian horsemen raided [[e:europe|Europe]] from [[e:saxony|Saxony]] to [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], until Otto I defeated them at the [[e:battle-of-lechfeld|Lechfeld]] in 955. The grand princes then centralised power: [[e:taksony|Taksony]] and especially [[e:geza-grand-prince-of-the-hungarians|Géza]], ruling from [[e:esztergom|Esztergom]], curbed tribal chiefs and invited Western missionaries. Géza was baptised and married his son [[e:stephen-i-of-hungary|Vajk]] to [[e:gisela-of-bavaria|Gisela of Bavaria]].
principality-of-hungary.e: [[e:geza-grand-prince-of-the-hungarians|Géza]]'s son [[e:stephen-i-of-hungary|Vajk]], baptised Stephen, defeated the pagan [[e:koppany|Koppány]] and was crowned king on Christmas Day 1000 (or 1 January 1001) with a crown from [[e:pope-sylvester-ii|Pope Sylvester II]], founding the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1000-1301).

prince-bishopric-of-geneva.t: The temporal lordship of the bishops of Geneva, whose loss to the citizens and the Reformation turned the city into the 'Protestant Rome' of Calvin.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.o: [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] had been a bishopric since the 4th century. In 1124 the Treaty of Seyssel between [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Humbert de Grammont and the Count of [[e:geneva|Geneva]] confirmed the bishop's lordship over the city, and [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] recognised him as an imperial prince in 1162.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled the city through officials, while the counts of [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] and later the dukes of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] held the vidomnat, an important judicial office. Citizens gained a charter of liberties from Bishop Adhémar Fabri in 1387. [[e:geneva|Geneva's]] fairs made it a major trading centre in the 15th century. Savoy princes increasingly held the bishopric itself.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.e: [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] allied with [[s:canton-of-fribourg|Fribourg]] and Bern in 1526, and in 1533 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:pierre-de-la-baume|Pierre de La Baume]] left the city. In 1535 to 1536 it adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and became an independent republic. [[e:john-calvin|John Calvin]] arrived in 1536. [[e:geneva|Geneva]] joined [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] in 1815.

pallava-dynasty.t: The dynasty of Kanchipuram that created the rock-cut temples of Mamallapuram and spread South Indian script and art across Southeast Asia.
pallava-dynasty.o: The Pallavas first appear in the 3rd and 4th centuries in [[e:prakrit|Prakrit]] charters from [[e:andhra-region|Andhra]] and the [[e:kanchipuram|Kanchipuram]] region, as the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] and the [[s:ikshvaku-dynasty|Ikshvaku dynasty]] declined. [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]] defeated a [[e:vishnugopa-of-kanchi|Vishnugopa of Kanchi]] in the 4th century. The dynasty became a major power after [[e:simhavishnu|Simhavishnu]] expelled the [[s:kalabhra-dynasty|Kalabhra dynasty]] from the Kaveri delta in the late 6th century.
pallava-dynasty.r: [[e:mahendravarman-i|Mahendravarman I]], a playwright who wrote the satire [[e:mattavilasa-prahasana|Mattavilasa]], built [[e:south-india|South India's]] first rock-cut temples and, according to tradition, turned from [[e:jainism|Jainism]] to [[e:shaivism|Shaivism]]. His son [[e:narasimhavarman-i|Narasimhavarman I]] took [[e:badami|Vatapi]] in 642, killing [[e:pulakeshin-ii|Pulakeshin II]] of the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]], and gave his name to the port of [[e:mamallapuram|Mamallapuram]], with its monolithic rathas. [[e:narasimhavarman-ii|Narasimhavarman II]] built the Shore Temple and the [[e:kailasanathar-temple-kanchipuram|Kailasanatha]] temple at [[e:kanchipuram|Kanchipuram]], a great centre of [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] learning.
pallava-dynasty.e: Weakened by wars with the [[e:chalukya-dynasty|Chalukyas]], [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakutas]] and [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Pandyas]], the Pallavas lost their kingdom when [[e:aparajitavarman|Aparajita]] was defeated by [[e:aditya-i|Aditya I]] of the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] around 897. [[e:pallava-script|Pallava Grantha]] script became the ancestor of many Southeast Asian alphabets.
