province-of-maine.t: A proprietary colony granted to Sir Ferdinando Gorges in what is now southern Maine, absorbed by Massachusetts in the 1650s.
province-of-maine.o: In 1622 the Council for [[e:new-england|New England]] granted [[e:ferdinando-gorges|Sir Ferdinando Gorges]] and [[e:john-mason-governor|John Mason]] the land between the [[e:merrimack-river|Merrimack]] and [[e:kennebec-river|Kennebec]] rivers. When they divided it in 1629, Gorges took the eastern part. Fishing stations and small settlements grew along the coast at [[e:kittery-maine|Kittery]], [[e:york-maine|York]] and [[e:saco-maine|Saco]], and in 1639 a royal charter made Gorges proprietor of the Province of [[s:county-of-maine|Maine]].
province-of-maine.r: [[e:ferdinando-gorges|Gorges]] never crossed the Atlantic, ruling through deputies such as his cousin [[e:thomas-gorges|Thomas Gorges]]. He planned an Anglican, manorial society and in 1641 chartered [[e:york-maine|York]] as Gorgeana, the first English city in America. In practice settlers lived from fishing, [[e:timber|timber]] and fur trading and quarrelled with the rival [[e:lygonia|Lygonia]] grant to the north. After Gorges died in 1647, the towns organised their own government.
province-of-maine.e: [[s:massachusetts-bay-colony|Massachusetts Bay Colony]] claimed that its charter covered the region and absorbed the towns between 1652 and 1658, organising them as [[e:yorkshire|Yorkshire]] County. [[s:province-of-massachusetts-bay|Massachusetts]] bought the [[e:ferdinando-gorges|Gorges]] heirs' claim in 1677, and [[s:county-of-maine|Maine]] remained part of Massachusetts until statehood in 1820.

pal-lahara-state.t: A small, hilly princely state in northern Odisha, one of the Orissa Tributary States until 1948.
pal-lahara-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but its origins are not reliably known.
pal-lahara-state.r: Pal Lahara was a thinly populated state of forest and hills, with [[e:bhuyan|Bhuyan]] and other Adivasi communities. It became one of the [[e:orissa-tributary-states|Orissa Tributary Mahals]] under British supervision after 1803. Its history is poorly recorded.
pal-lahara-state.e: Pal Lahara merged into [[e:odisha|Orissa]] on 1 January 1948 and is now in [[e:angul-district|Angul district]].

principality-of-capua.t: Lombard principality of northern Campania that broke away from Benevento and later became the first Norman principality in southern Italy.
principality-of-capua.o: In the civil wars of the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] south in the 840s, [[e:landulf-i-of-capua|Landulf I]], gastald of [[s:capua|Capua]], made his town practically independent of both [[e:benevento|Benevento]] and [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]]. Arab raiders destroyed old Capua in 841, and in 856 his family founded a new Capua on the site of [[e:casilinum|Casilinum]] by the [[e:volturno|Volturno]]. Its rulers took the title of prince by the early 10th century.
principality-of-capua.r: [[s:capua|Capua]] was ruled by quarrelsome branches of [[e:landulf-i-of-capua|Landulf]]'s family, who controlled northern [[e:campania|Campania]] and much of the Liri valley. [[e:pandulf-ironhead|Pandulf Ironhead]] (died 981) briefly united Capua, [[e:benevento|Benevento]] and [[e:spoleto|Spoleto]] under imperial patronage. [[e:pandulf-iv-of-capua|Pandulf IV]], called the Wolf of the [[e:abruzzo|Abruzzi]], despoiled [[e:monte-cassino|Monte Cassino]] and, like his rivals, hired Norman [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], helping the Normans gain a foothold in Campania.
principality-of-capua.e: The Norman [[e:richard-i-of-england|Richard I]] of [[s:county-of-aversa|Aversa]] took [[s:capua|Capua]] in 1058, and his family ruled it as princes for nearly eighty years. After [[e:robert-ii-of-capua|Robert II of Capua]] resisted [[e:roger-ii-of-sicily|Roger II]], the principality was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]] in 1135.

principality-of-isenburg.t: Hessian principality of the Isenburg-Birstein line that rose to sovereignty under Napoleon only to be mediatised at Vienna.
principality-of-isenburg.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] had held lands in the [[e:wetterau|Wetterau]] and around [[e:budingen|Büdingen]] since the [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]], divided into many lines. The Birstein branch was raised to princely rank in 1744 under Wolfgang Ernst I, ruling from Birstein Castle in the [[e:vogelsberg|Vogelsberg]] foothills.
principality-of-isenburg.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with [[e:offenbach-am-main|Offenbach am Main]] as its most important town, where [[e:huguenots|Huguenot]] settlers had built crafts and trade. [[e:charles-prince-of-isenburg|Prince Charles]] joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1806, gaining full [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] and absorbing the lands of other [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] lines, and supplied a regiment to [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] army.
principality-of-isenburg.e: After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] fall [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] was occupied by the allies, and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] mediatised it. In 1816 its lands were divided between the [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Grand Duchy of Hesse]] and the [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Electorate of Hesse]], the princes keeping their estates.

cr.a: Gustav Droysen; derivative work by Beckstet

prince-abbey-of-fulda.t: Abbey founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, a centre of Carolingian learning, and later a baroque prince-bishopric in eastern Hesse.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.o: [[e:sturmi|Sturm]], a disciple of [[e:saint-boniface|Saint Boniface]], founded the monastery at [[e:fulda|Fulda]] in 744, and Boniface was buried there in 754. Under Abbot [[e:hrabanus-maurus|Hrabanus Maurus]] in the 9th century it became one of the great centres of learning in the Frankish realm. Its abbots gathered vast estates and were recognised as imperial princes by 1220.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.r: The prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory in the [[e:rhon|Rhön]] and the [[e:fulda|Fulda]] valley, with the support of a powerful noble chapter. Abbot [[e:balthasar-von-dernbach|Balthasar von Dernbach]] led a fierce [[e:counter-reformation|Counter-Reformation]] in the late 16th century. The baroque cathedral by [[e:johann-dientzenhofer|Johann Dientzenhofer]] and the abbots' palace reshaped the town, and in 1752 the abbey was raised to a prince-bishopric.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.e: Secularised in 1802, Fulda went to [[e:william-i-of-the-netherlands|William Frederick of Nassau-Orange]], then to French control and the [[s:grand-duchy-of-frankfurt|Grand Duchy of Frankfurt]]. In 1816 it passed to the [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Electorate of Hesse]]. The diocese of [[e:fulda|Fulda]] continues today.

piedras-negras.t: A Classic Maya kingdom on the Usumacinta whose stelae enabled Tatiana Proskouriakoff to prove in 1960 that Maya inscriptions record real history.
piedras-negras.o: Piedras Negras, anciently Yo'k'ib', occupied the Guatemalan bank of the [[e:usumacinta-river|Usumacinta]], upstream from [[s:yaxchilan|Yaxchilan]]. Its kings appear in inscriptions from the 5th century, around 460 CE, and the city fought long wars with Yaxchilan over the river valley.
piedras-negras.r: From the early 7th century its rulers raised a series of stelae marking accessions, showing a king seated in a niche above a ladder. Analysing these sequences, [[e:tatiana-proskouriakoff|Proskouriakoff]] demonstrated that the glyphs named rulers and dated events in their lives. The kingdom was often allied with the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]] and built sweat baths, palaces and a fine carved throne.
piedras-negras.e: In 808 [[s:yaxchilan|Yaxchilan]] captured [[e:kinich-yat-ahk-ii|K'inich Yat Ahk II]], the last known king, and the city declined swiftly, being abandoned by the early 9th century. Excavations in the 1930s and 1990s revealed much of its layout.

phocian-league.t: Federation of the towns of Phocis in central Greece, which seized Delphi and fought the Third Sacred War against Thebes and Philip II.
phocian-league.o: The Phocians lived in the valley of the [[e:cephissus-boeotia|Cephissus]] and around [[e:mount-parnassus|Mount Parnassus]], in some twenty small towns such as [[e:elateia|Elateia]]. By the 6th century BCE they formed a federation with a common council house, the Phokikon. Their long wars with the Thessalians included famous stratagems with chalk-whitened warriors.
phocian-league.r: [[e:phocis|Phocis]] guarded the path around [[e:battle-of-thermopylae|Thermopylae]] and fought in 480 BCE before submitting to [[e:persia|Persia]]. In 356 BCE, fined by the Amphictyony, the Phocians under [[e:philomelus|Philomelus]] seized [[s:delphi|Delphi]] and used its treasure to hire [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]]. [[e:onomarchus|Onomarchus]] twice defeated [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]] in 353 BCE but was killed at the [[e:battle-of-the-crocus-field|Battle of the Crocus Field]] in 352 BCE.
phocian-league.e: In 346 BCE [[e:phalaecus|Phalaecus]] surrendered to [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]]. The Phocian towns were broken into villages, [[e:phocis|Phocis]] lost its vote in the Amphictyony and owed annual indemnities to [[s:delphi|Delphi]]. It later revived as a league.

principality-of-khachen.t: An Armenian principality in the highlands of Karabakh that survived Arab, Seljuk and Mongol overlords for nearly eight centuries and built the monastery of Gandzasar.
principality-of-khachen.o: Khachen emerged in the 9th century in the mountains of [[e:artsakh-historic-province|Artsakh]], in the former lands of the [[s:mihranid-principality-of-albania|Mihranid Principality of Albania]]. Its early prince [[e:sahl-smbatean|Sahl Smbatean]] became famous for capturing the rebel leader [[e:babak-khorramdin|Babak]] in 837 and handing him to the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasids]]. The principality took its name from the fortress of Khachen.
principality-of-khachen.r: Princes ruled from mountain fortresses such as Khokhanaberd over Armenian villages, vineyards and monasteries. The greatest, [[e:hasan-jalal-dawla|Hasan-Jalal Dawla]], prince from 1214, built the monastery of [[e:gandzasar-monastery|Gandzasar]], seat of the Catholicos of [[s:caucasian-albania|Aghvank]]. Khachen served as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[s:zakarid-armenia|Zakarid Armenia]], the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] and the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], keeping local autonomy through skilful diplomacy and [[e:diplomatic-marriage|dynastic marriages]].
principality-of-khachen.e: After [[e:hasan-jalal-dawla|Hasan-Jalal]]'s execution by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1261, Khachen fragmented among branches of his house. Under the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] in the early 17th century its lands were reorganised into the [[s:melikdoms-of-karabakh|Melikdoms of Karabakh]], among them Khachen itself, still ruled by descendants of the [[e:house-of-hasan-jalalyan|Hasan-Jalalyan]] family.

prince-bishopric-of-worms.t: A small prince-bishopric on the upper Rhine whose bishops lost their city of Worms and ruled a few scattered lands from Ladenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.o: [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]] had been a bishopric since Roman times. [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:burchard-of-worms|Burchard of Worms]], who issued a famous collection of canon law around 1020, gained wide rights over the city. In 1156 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] confirmed the bishop's possessions, and the bishops became princes of a small territory.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] lost control of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]] itself, which became a free imperial city; the [[e:concordat-of-worms|Concordat of Worms]] in 1122 and [[e:martin-luther|Luther]]'s appearance at the [[e:diet-of-worms|Diet of Worms]] in 1521 took place there. The bishops ruled scattered lands, sharing [[e:ladenburg|Ladenburg]] with the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]]. The see was often held together with [[e:mainz|Mainz]].
prince-bishopric-of-worms.e: [[e:france|France]] annexed the left-bank lands in the 1790s, and in 1803 the remaining territories were secularised and given to [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]] and [[e:baden|Baden]]. The diocese itself was dissolved in 1801 and later merged into the diocese of [[e:mainz|Mainz]].

principality-of-bryansk.t: A forest principality on the Desna that inherited the senior role in the Chernigov lands after the Mongol sack, before falling to Lithuania.
principality-of-bryansk.o: [[e:bryansk|Bryansk]] on the [[e:desna-river|Desna]] was a town of the [[s:principality-of-chernigov|Principality of Chernigov]]. After the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] destroyed [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] in 1239 and [[e:mikhail-of-chernigov|Prince Mikhail]] was killed in 1246, his son [[e:roman-mikhailovich-of-bryansk|Roman Mikhailovich]] made Bryansk his seat, and it became the leading principality of the old Chernigov lands.
principality-of-bryansk.r: Protected by thick forests, [[e:bryansk|Bryansk]] recovered more quickly than the open lands to the south. [[e:roman-mikhailovich-of-bryansk|Roman Mikhailovich]], who ruled until the 1280s, fought off Lithuanian raids and allied by marriage with the princes of [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia|Galicia-Volhynia]]. From the early 14th century princes of the [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] line held the town, and it was torn by disputes between pro-Lithuanian and pro-Horde factions.
principality-of-bryansk.e: Around 1356 [[e:algirdas|Algirdas]] of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] took [[e:bryansk|Bryansk]] and later gave it to his son Dmitry. It remained Lithuanian until the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] took it in 1500.

principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.t: A Thuringian principality of the house of Schwarzburg, ruled from Sondershausen and Arnstadt, where the young Bach held his first organ post.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.o: The [[e:treaty-of-stadtilm|Treaty of Stadtilm]] of 1599 split the [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]] lands, and Count [[e:john-gunther-i-of-schwarzburg-sondershausen|John Günther I]]'s line received [[e:sondershausen|Sondershausen]] and [[e:arnstadt|Arnstadt]], forming Schwarzburg-Sondershausen alongside the [[s:principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt|Principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt]].
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.r: The counts became princes in 1697 and ruled a Lutheran territory in two parts, the Lower Lordship around [[e:sondershausen|Sondershausen]] and the Upper Lordship around [[e:arnstadt|Arnstadt]]. Arnstadt gave [[e:johann-sebastian-bach|Johann Sebastian Bach]] his first post as organist in 1703. The princes kept a court orchestra, and in the 19th century Sondershausen became known for its public concerts and music school.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.e: The principality joined the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] in 1871. When Prince [[e:karl-gunther-prince-of-schwarzburg-sondershausen|Karl Günther]] died childless in 1909, [[e:gunther-victor-prince-of-schwarzburg|Günther Victor of Rudolstadt]] inherited it in personal union. He abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the [[s:free-state-of-thuringia|Free State of Thuringia]].

principality-of-reuss-schleiz.t: Branch of the Reuss family in Thuringia that eventually reunited the Younger Line of Reuss under its rule.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.o: Reuss-[[e:schleiz|Schleiz]] was created in the 1647 division of the Younger Line of the [[e:house-of-reuss|House of Reuss]], centred on the town of Schleiz. The counts, descended from the medieval [[e:vogt|Vögte]] of [[e:weida|Weida]], Gera and [[e:plauen|Plauen]], held small territories in eastern [[e:thuringia|Thuringia]].
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with textile crafts, and its counts, all named Heinrich, ruled through a Lutheran church and a small court at [[e:schleiz|Schleiz]]. The Schleiz line was raised to princely rank in 1806, joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and then the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]], and shared the inheritance of [[e:principality-of-reuss-younger-line|Reuss-Gera]] when that line died out in 1802.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.e: In 1848, after the abdication of the Prince of [[s:principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf|Reuss-Lobenstein-Ebersdorf]], the [[e:schleiz|Schleiz]] line united all lands of the Younger Line as the [[e:principality-of-reuss-younger-line|Principality of Reuss Younger Line]], with Gera as capital. That state survived until 1918 and became part of the [[s:peoples-state-of-reuss|People's State of Reuss]].

pushyabhuti-dynasty.t: The dynasty of Harsha, who ruled much of northern India from Kannauj in the 7th century and was described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.
pushyabhuti-dynasty.o: The Pushyabhutis ruled [[s:thanesar-state|Thanesar]], north of [[e:delhi|Delhi]], from around 500. [[e:prabhakaravardhana|Prabhakaravardhana]] made them a regional power in the late 6th century. After his death his elder son [[e:rajyavardhana|Rajyavardhana]] was murdered by [[e:shashanka|Shashanka]] of the [[s:gauda-kingdom|Gauda Kingdom]], and in 606 his younger brother [[e:harsha|Harsha]] took the throne, also inheriting the kingdom of the [[s:maukharis|Maukharis]] at [[e:kannauj|Kannauj]].
pushyabhuti-dynasty.r: [[e:harsha|Harsha]] campaigned across northern [[e:india|India]], though [[e:pulakeshin-ii|Pulakeshin II]] of the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]] stopped him at the [[e:narmada-river|Narmada]]. He governed through [[e:vassal|vassal]] kings, toured his realm and held great religious assemblies at [[e:kannauj|Kannauj]] and [[e:prayagraj|Prayag]]. A patron of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] and of [[e:shaivism|Shaiva]] and Sun cults, he wrote three [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] plays, and his court poet [[e:banabhatta|Banabhatta]] composed the [[e:harshacharita|Harshacharita]]. Harsha exchanged embassies with [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]].
pushyabhuti-dynasty.e: [[e:harsha|Harsha]] died in 647 without an heir, and his empire collapsed at once. A minister seized [[e:kannauj|Kannauj]], and northern [[e:india|India]] broke into rival states until the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]] rose in the 8th century.

principality-of-samarkand.t: The leading Sogdian city-state, ruled by ikhshids whose merchants ran Silk Road trade networks from Byzantium to China.
principality-of-samarkand.o: [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]], ancient Maracanda, had been the chief city of Sogdiana since Achaemenid times. After the fall of the [[s:hephthalite-empire|Hephthalite Empire]] it emerged in the 6th century as the foremost of the Sogdian principalities under rulers with the title ikhshid, recognising the overlordship of the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]].
principality-of-samarkand.r: The ikhshids presided over a merchant aristocracy rather than an absolute monarchy. Sogdian traders dominated [[e:caravan-trade|caravan commerce]] across [[e:asia|Asia]], with communities in [[e:china|China]] and [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]]. The famous murals of [[e:afrasiab|Afrasiab]], painted for the ruler [[e:varkhuman|Varkhuman]] around 660, show embassies from China, [[e:korea|Korea]] and the Turks. Religion was a local [[e:zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] with [[e:fire-temple|fire temples]] and ossuary burial, alongside [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]], [[e:manichaeism|Manichaeism]] and [[e:christianity|Christianity]].
principality-of-samarkand.e: [[e:qutayba-ibn-muslim|Qutayba ibn Muslim]] took [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]] for the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] in 712, and the ikhshid [[e:ghurak|Ghurak]] ruled as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] while also courting the [[s:turgesh-khaganate|Turgesh Khaganate]]. After the Abbasid takeover around 750 the ikhshids lost power, and the city passed to the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanid Empire]] in the 9th century.

principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.t: A papal enclave in southern Italy that Napoleon turned into a sovereign principality for his foreign minister Talleyrand.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.o: [[e:benevento|Benevento]], a small city surrounded by the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]], had belonged to the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] since the 11th century. In 1806 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] seized it and made [[e:charles-maurice-de-talleyrand|Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand]], his foreign minister, sovereign Prince of Benevento.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.r: [[e:charles-maurice-de-talleyrand|Talleyrand]] never visited his principality. He ruled through a governor, Louis de Beer, who introduced French-style administration and the [[e:napoleonic-code|Napoleonic Code]], abolished feudal privileges and improved roads and finances. The small state continued to depend on the [[s:kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815|Napoleonic Kingdom of Naples]] (1806–1815) around it.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.e: With [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] fall, [[e:charles-maurice-de-talleyrand|Talleyrand]] gave up the title, and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] returned [[e:benevento|Benevento]] to the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] in 1815. It remained papal until 1860.

provisional-government-of-cuba.t: The second US occupation of Cuba, from 1906 to 1909, invoked under the Platt Amendment after a revolt against President Estrada Palma.
provisional-government-of-cuba.o: [[e:tomas-estrada-palma|Tomás Estrada Palma's]] disputed re-election in 1906 provoked a Liberal revolt in August. Estrada [[e:palma|Palma]] asked for US help and then resigned, leaving [[e:cuba|Cuba]] without a government. Under the [[e:platt-amendment|Platt Amendment]], [[e:theodore-roosevelt|Theodore Roosevelt]] sent Secretary of War [[e:william-howard-taft|William Howard Taft]], who proclaimed a provisional government in September 1906.
provisional-government-of-cuba.r: [[e:william-howard-taft|Taft]] was soon replaced by [[e:charles-magoon|Charles Magoon]], who governed until 1909 while preserving [[e:cuba|Cuba's]] flag and laws. Magoon used government jobs and contracts to buy peace among Cuban factions, built roads and public works, created a permanent army and drafted new electoral laws. Critics accused his administration of waste and of draining the surplus left by [[e:tomas-estrada-palma|Estrada Palma]].
provisional-government-of-cuba.e: Elections in 1908 were won by the Liberal [[e:jose-miguel-gomez|José Miguel Gómez]], who took office on 28 January 1909, restoring the [[s:republic-of-cuba-1902-1959|Republic of Cuba]] (1902-1959). The occupation confirmed US influence over Cuban politics for decades.

pella.t: Pella, a Canaanite town in the Jordan Valley known to the Egyptians as Pihilu, whose rulers wrote to the pharaoh in the Amarna age.
pella.o: Pihilu stood at Tabaqat Fahl, beside a perennial spring above the [[s:hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan|Jordan]] Valley, inhabited since the [[e:neolithic|Neolithic]]. In the [[e:middle-bronze-age|Middle Bronze Age]] it became a walled town, named in Egyptian execration texts, and controlled farmland and the route from the valley into the [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Transjordan]] highlands.
pella.r: [[e:university-of-sydney|University of Sydney]] excavations since 1979 have uncovered fortifications, a [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] governor's residence and a temple. In the 14th century BCE its ruler Mut-Bahlu wrote to the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] in the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], and Akkadian tablets have been found at the site.
pella.e: The Canaanite town declined with Egyptian power in the 12th century BCE. Pella revived in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] and became one of the cities of the [[s:decapolis-levant|Decapolis (Levant)]].

pale-of-calais.t: England's last foothold in mainland France, a fortified port and wool staple held for two centuries after Edward III's siege of 1346–1347.
pale-of-calais.o: After his victory at [[e:battle-of-crecy|Crécy]], [[e:edward-iii-of-england|Edward III]] besieged Calais for eleven months and took it in 1347; the story of the six [[e:burghers|burghers]] who offered their lives is famous. The English expelled much of the population and settled the town with English colonists, adding a surrounding district of marsh and forts, the Pale.
pale-of-calais.r: Calais was garrisoned by the largest standing force of the English crown. From 1363 it hosted the Staple, through which [[e:england|England's]] raw wool exports passed, and the Merchants of the Staple funded its defence. From 1536 it sent members to the English Parliament. It was a base for English armies in [[e:france|France]] for two centuries.
pale-of-calais.e: In January 1558, during a war in alliance with [[e:spain|Spain]], Francis, duke of Guise, captured Calais in a surprise winter attack. [[e:mary-i-of-england|Mary I]] reportedly said that Calais would be found written on her heart. [[e:the-pale|The Pale]] became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

patria-vieja.t: Chile's first period of self-government, from the junta of 1810 to the royalist victory at Rancagua in 1814.
patria-vieja.o: On 18 September 1810, a date still celebrated as Chile's national day, a cabildo in [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] created a governing junta led by the elderly [[e:mateo-de-toro-zambrano|Mateo de Toro Zambrano]], ruling in the name of the captive [[e:ferdinand-vii-of-spain|Ferdinand VII]]. It replaced the governor of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-chile|Captaincy General of Chile]].
patria-vieja.r: The junta opened ports to free trade and convened the [[e:first-national-congress-of-chile|First National Congress]] in 1811. [[e:jose-miguel-carrera|José Miguel Carrera]] seized power in a series of coups and introduced a provisional constitution, the first national flag and the newspaper [[e:aurora-de-chile|Aurora de Chile]], edited by [[e:camilo-henriquez|Camilo Henríquez]]. Divisions between the Carreras and [[e:bernardo-ohiggins|Bernardo O'Higgins]] weakened the patriots as the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] of [[e:peru|Peru]], [[e:jose-fernando-de-abascal|José Fernando de Abascal]], sent troops in 1813.
patria-vieja.e: The [[e:treaty-of-lircay|Treaty of Lircay]] in 1814 briefly halted the war. Royalist forces then defeated [[e:bernardo-ohiggins|O'Higgins]] at [[e:battle-of-rancagua|Rancagua]] in October 1814, and the patriots fled to [[e:mendoza-argentina|Mendoza]]. The [[e:reconquista|Reconquista]] lasted until [[e:battle-of-chacabuco|Chacabuco]] in 1817.

pashalik-of-scutari.t: Semi-independent Ottoman province of the Bushati family in northern Albania, whose pashas waged their own wars and defied the sultan for decades.
pashalik-of-scutari.o: [[e:mehmed-pasha-bushati|Mehmed Pasha Bushati]], from a powerful [[e:shkoder|Shkodër]] family, was appointed governor of the sanjak of Scutari in 1757 and made the post hereditary in practice. The [[e:bushati-family|Bushatis]] used the weakness of central Ottoman government in the later 18th century to build an autonomous domain over northern [[s:albania|Albania]] and parts of [[s:montenegro|Montenegro]] and [[e:kosovo|Kosovo]].
pashalik-of-scutari.r: The pashas ruled through Albanian clan chiefs and their own armies, collecting taxes and trading with [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]]. Mehmed built the [[e:lead-mosque-shkoder|Lead Mosque]] at [[e:shkoder|Shkodër]] in 1773. [[e:kara-mahmud-pasha-bushati|Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati]] expanded the domain, negotiated directly with [[e:austria|Austria]] and fought the Ottoman government, but was killed fighting the Montenegrins at [[e:battle-of-krusi|Krusi]] in 1796. Catholic and Muslim [[e:albanians|Albanians]] coexisted.
pashalik-of-scutari.e: [[e:mustafa-pasha-bushati|Mustafa Pasha Bushati]], the last ruler, joined Bosnian notables against the reforms of [[e:mahmud-ii|Mahmud II]]. In 1831 the grand [[e:vizier|vizier]] [[e:resid-mehmed-pasha|Reşid Mehmed Pasha]] defeated him and forced his surrender at [[e:rozafa-castle|Rozafa]] castle, restoring direct Ottoman rule over [[e:shkoder|Shkodër]].

peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.t: The Vietnamese-backed Cambodian state established after the overthrow of the Khmer Rouge in 1979, isolated internationally for a decade.
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.o: After [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] invaded [[s:democratic-kampuchea|Democratic Kampuchea]], its forces took [[e:phnom-penh|Phnom Penh]] on 7 January 1979, and the People's Republic of [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia|Kampuchea]] was proclaimed, led by the [[e:kampuchean-united-front-for-national-salvation|Kampuchean United Front for National Salvation]], a group of former [[e:khmer-rouge|Khmer Rouge]] cadres who had defected to [[e:vietnam|Vietnam]], including [[e:heng-samrin|Heng Samrin]] and [[e:hun-sen|Hun Sen]].
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.r: The PRK was a one-party state under the [[e:cambodian-peoples-party|Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party]], with Vietnamese troops and advisers. It reopened schools, markets, pagodas and [[e:phnom-penh|Phnom Penh]] itself, and gathered evidence of [[e:khmer-rouge|Khmer Rouge]] crimes at [[e:tuol-sleng|Tuol Sleng]]. It faced famine in 1979 to 1980 and a [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] war from a coalition of the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] Rouge, royalists and republicans, which held [[e:cambodia|Cambodia's]] UN seat.
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.e: As Soviet aid declined, [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] prepared to withdraw its troops, completed in 1989. That year the state was renamed the [[s:state-of-cambodia|State of Cambodia]], dropping some socialist features to prepare for a negotiated settlement.

cr.a: See File History, below, for details.

principality-of-murom.t: An old principality on the Oka, home of the legend of Peter and Fevronia, later absorbed into Moscow's growing realm.
principality-of-murom.o: [[e:murom|Murom]], named after the Finnic [[e:muroma|Muroma]] tribe, is mentioned in the [[e:primary-chronicle|Primary Chronicle]] under 862. [[e:vladimir-the-great|Vladimir I]]'s son [[e:boris-and-gleb|Gleb]], later venerated as a saint, held it in the early 11th century. It became the seat of the descendants of [[e:yaroslav-sviatoslavich|Yaroslav Sviatoslavich]] of [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], and around 1127 split from the neighbouring [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Grand Principality of Ryazan]] to form a separate principality.
principality-of-murom.r: [[e:murom|Murom]] was a frontier town on the [[e:oka-river|Oka]], close to [[s:volga-bulgaria|Volga Bulgaria]] and the forest peoples, and lived from trade and farming. Its princes were usually overshadowed by [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]]. The tale of Prince Peter and the peasant healer [[e:peter-and-fevronia-of-murom|Fevronia]], venerated as patrons of marriage, is set here, as is the epic hero [[e:ilya-muromets|Ilya Muromets]].
principality-of-murom.e: The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] sacked [[e:murom|Murom]] in 1239, and it declined into a minor dependent principality. In 1392 Vasily I of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] bought from the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] the right to rule Murom along with [[e:nizhny-novgorod|Nizhny Novgorod]], ending its independence.

prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.t: Small Mecklenburg church state founded during the conversion of the Obotrites and absorbed by the dukes of Mecklenburg after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.o: The bishopric was set up by [[e:henry-the-lion|Henry the Lion]] during the conquest of the Slavic [[s:obotrite-confederation|Obotrites]], with the Cistercian monk [[e:berno-of-schwerin|Berno]] as its first [[e:bishop|bishop]] and its seat moved to [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] around 1160. After [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] fall in 1180 the bishops held their estates as imperial princes, a status the dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] constantly disputed.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.r: The territory was small, consisting chiefly of lands around [[e:butzow|Bützow]], where the [[e:bishop|bishops]] resided, and Warin. It grew through German settlement in former Slavic lands. In the 16th century the see was held by princes of the [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] house, such as [[e:ulrich-duke-of-mecklenburg|Ulrich of Mecklenburg]], and became Lutheran, so the bishopric functioned in practice as a Mecklenburg [[e:appanage|appanage]].
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 secularised it as the Principality of [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] and awarded it to the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] as compensation for [[s:swedish-wismar|Wismar]], which went to [[e:sweden|Sweden]]. It is now part of [[e:mecklenburg-vorpommern|Mecklenburg-Vorpommern]].

protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.t: The British protectorate built on the conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate, where Frederick Lugard developed the system of indirect rule through the emirs.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.o: On 1 January 1900 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took over the northern lands of the [[s:royal-niger-company-territories|Royal Niger Company]] and proclaimed the [[e:northern-nigeria-protectorate|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]], with [[e:frederick-lugard|Frederick Lugard]] as high commissioner. Its capital was first [[e:lokoja|Lokoja]] and from 1902 [[e:zungeru|Zungeru]]. Between 1900 and 1903 British-led troops conquered the [[e:emirate|emirates]], taking [[e:kano|Kano]] and [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]] in 1903.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.r: With few officials and little money, [[e:frederick-lugard|Lugard]] governed through the [[e:emir|emirs]] who accepted British authority, keeping their courts, taxes and officials under the supervision of British residents. This [[e:indirect-rule|indirect rule]], set out in his Political Memoranda, became a model for British [[e:africa|Africa]]. Christian missions were restricted in Muslim areas, and Western schooling spread slowly. A revolt at [[e:satiru-uprising|Satiru]] in 1906 was crushed.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.e: [[e:frederick-lugard|Lugard]] returned as governor of both [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] in 1912 and merged them on 1 January 1914 into [[s:colonial-nigeria|Colonial Nigeria]]. The north remained a separate administrative region, and the legacy of separate development shaped Nigerian politics.

principality-of-nassau-siegen.t: Iron-mining Nassau principality in the Siegerland, divided for a century between Catholic and Protestant branches of the house.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.o: After the death of Count [[e:john-vi-count-of-nassau-dillenburg|John VI]] of [[s:county-of-nassau-dillenburg|Nassau-Dillenburg]] in 1606, his lands were divided and his son [[e:john-vii-count-of-nassau-siegen|John VII]] received [[e:siegen|Siegen]]. Siegen was the birthplace of [[e:peter-paul-rubens|Peter Paul Rubens]] in 1577, when his parents lived there in exile.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.r: The [[e:siegerland|Siegerland's]] iron ore and forges made it relatively prosperous. The house split confessionally: [[e:john-viii-count-of-nassau-siegen|John VIII]] converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and his line held part of the land while the Reformed line held the rest, so [[e:siegen|Siegen]] had two castles, the Upper and Lower. [[e:johan-maurits-of-nassau-siegen|Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen]], governor of [[s:dutch-brazil|Dutch Brazil]], belonged to the Reformed branch. Counts became princes in 1652 and 1664.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.e: The Reformed line died out in 1734 and the Catholic line in 1743, and the territory passed to Prince [[e:william-iv-prince-of-orange|William IV of Orange-Nassau]] as part of [[s:principality-of-nassau-diez|Nassau-Diez]]. It later went to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-berg|Grand Duchy of Berg]] and in 1815 to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]].

principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.t: Swabian territory acquired by the family that ran the Imperial Post, giving them a vote among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.o: The Taxis family of [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] origin had run the imperial postal service since around 1500 and became hereditary postmasters general, raised to princes in 1695. To gain a seat in the [[e:council-of-princes|Council of Princes]] they needed land, so in 1785 they bought the county of Friedberg-Scheer on the [[e:danube|Danube]], raised in 1786 to a princely county.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.r: The Swabian territory was a small Catholic rural district; the family's wealth and power came from the Imperial Post, which carried letters across the Empire and the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]]. The princes lived in [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]], where they represented the emperor as principal commissioner at the [[e:imperial-diet|Perpetual Imperial Diet]], and from 1812 resided in the former [[e:st-emmerams-abbey|St Emmeram Abbey]].
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.e: In 1806 the territory was mediatised under the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. The family kept its postal business in many German states until selling it to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1867 and remains among the largest landowners in [[e:germany|Germany]].

principality-of-gjirokaster.t: Albanian lordship of the Zenebishi family in southern Albania, one of the last Christian powers in Epirus before the Ottoman conquest.
principality-of-gjirokaster.o: [[e:gjon-zenebishi|Gjon Zenebishi]], an Albanian chieftain whose clan had moved into [[e:epirus|Epirus]] during the 14th-century Albanian migrations, took the fortress of [[e:gjirokaster|Gjirokastër]] (Argyrokastron) around 1386. He extended his rule over the [[e:drino|Drino]] valley and parts of [[e:chameria|Chameria]], and the Byzantine court recognised him with the title of sebastokrator.
principality-of-gjirokaster.r: The lordship was a clan-based military domain built around the hilltop citadel of [[e:gjirokaster|Gjirokastër]] and its villages. Gjon fought the Italian rulers of the [[s:despotate-of-epirus|Despotate of Epirus]] at [[e:ioannina|Ioannina]], capturing [[e:esau-de-buondelmonti|Esau de' Buondelmonti]] in 1399, and courted [[e:venice|Venice]], which controlled nearby [[s:corcyra|Corfu]]. Society rested on Albanian pastoral clans and an [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Greek and Albanian peasantry.
principality-of-gjirokaster.e: Repeated Ottoman campaigns under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mehmed I wore the lordship down, and [[e:gjirokaster|Gjirokastër]] fell in 1418, the year Gjon died. His son Depa fled to Venetian territory and later led a failed rising in 1434. The town became the centre of an Ottoman sanjak.

principality-of-tmutarakan.t: A remote outpost of Kievan Rus' on the Taman peninsula, controlling the strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
principality-of-tmutarakan.o: Tmutarakan grew out of the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] town of Tamatarkha, on the site of ancient [[e:hermonassa|Hermonassa]]. After [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav I]] broke Khazar power in the 960s, the Rus' took control, and around 988 Vladimir I gave the town to his son Mstislav as his own principality.
principality-of-tmutarakan.r: Its population of [[e:greeks|Greeks]], [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]], [[s:alans|Alans]], [[e:kasogs|Kasogs]] and [[e:slavs|Slavs]] lived by trade between the steppe, the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. Mstislav defeated the Kasog prince [[e:rededya|Rededya]] in single combat in 1022, and in 1024 beat his brother Yaroslav at [[e:battle-of-listven|Listven]], dividing Rus' along the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]]. The Tmutarakan Stone records Prince [[e:gleb-sviatoslavich|Gleb]] measuring the frozen strait in 1068.
principality-of-tmutarakan.e: Tmutarakan served as a refuge for exiled princes such as [[e:oleg-sviatoslavich|Oleg Sviatoslavich]], who left it in 1094 to fight for [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]]. Cut off by the [[e:cumans|Cumans]], it disappears from Rus' history afterwards, probably passing to Byzantine control. Its location was rediscovered in the 18th century.

prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.t: A Benedictine abbey on the Jagst that was converted in 1460 into a provostry of noble canons whose princes ruled a sizeable Swabian territory.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.o: [[e:ellwangen|Ellwangen]] abbey was founded around 764 by Hariolf, later [[e:bishop|bishop]] of [[e:langres|Langres]], and received Carolingian protection. It built up lands along the [[e:jagst|Jagst]], and its abbots held princely rank from the 13th century. In 1460 [[e:pope-pius-ii|Pope Pius II]] converted the abbey into a secular collegiate foundation headed by a prince-provost.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.r: The prince-provost, often a [[e:bishop|bishop]] elsewhere as well, governed a considerable territory around [[e:ellwangen|Ellwangen]] with his own courts and officials and sat among the ecclesiastical princes of the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. The castle above the town was his residence. Witch trials between 1611 and 1618 were among the most severe in [[e:germany|Germany]], claiming several hundred victims.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.e: In 1802 and 1803 the provostry was secularised and annexed by Württemberg, which for some years made [[e:ellwangen|Ellwangen]] the seat of the government of its new Catholic lands. The castle and the Romanesque collegiate basilica survive.

puruha.t: A highland people of central Ecuador around Chimborazo who were absorbed by the Incas and later by the Spanish, but whose identity survives today.
puruha.o: The Puruhá occupied the highland basin around the volcano [[e:chimborazo|Chimborazo]], in the modern provinces of Chimborazo and [[e:bolivar-province-ecuador|Bolívar]], from around 800. Archaeology shows a sequence of local pottery traditions, with the Puruhá phase often linked to tombs found near [[e:riobamba|Riobamba]].
puruha.r: Little is known of their political organisation beyond a series of chiefdoms under local lords. They farmed [[e:maize|maize]], [[e:potato|potatoes]] and quinoa on the volcanic slopes and herded llamas. Their tombs contained [[e:copper|copper]] ornaments and distinctive pottery, including vessels with modelled human faces. Later chroniclers claimed that Puruhá lords allied by marriage with [[e:quito|Quito]], but these accounts are doubtful.
puruha.e: The Puruhá were brought under [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] rule around 1470 during the campaigns of [[e:tupac-inca-yupanqui|Túpac Inca Yupanqui]]. After the Spanish conquest, [[e:riobamba|Riobamba]] was founded in their territory in 1534. Their descendants, Kichwa-speaking communities of [[e:chimborazo|Chimborazo]], keep a strong indigenous identity.

prince-abbey-of-corvey.t: The leading Carolingian abbey of Saxony, a base for missions to the north and home of the chronicler Widukind, whose westwork is a World Heritage Site.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.o: Corvey was founded in 822 on the [[e:weser|Weser]] near [[e:hoxter|Höxter]] by monks from [[e:corbie-abbey|Corbie]] in [[e:picardy|Picardy]], led by [[e:adalard-of-corbie|Adalard]] and Wala, cousins of [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]], with the support of [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]]. It was intended to anchor [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in newly conquered [[e:saxony|Saxony]], and in 836 it received the relics of [[e:saint-vitus|Saint Vitus]] from [[e:basilica-of-saint-denis|Saint-Denis]].
prince-abbey-of-corvey.r: Corvey sent [[e:ansgar|Ansgar]] on his mission to [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:sweden|Sweden]], and its school produced [[e:widukind-of-corvey|Widukind of Corvey]], whose Deeds of the [[s:saxons|Saxons]] is a chief source for the Ottonian kings. The abbots were princes of the Empire ruling a small territory around [[e:hoxter|Höxter]]. Its Carolingian westwork, completed in 885, is one of the few surviving from the period.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.e: Corvey shrank after the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. In 1792 it was raised to a prince-bishopric, but in 1803 it was secularised and given to the Prince of Orange-Nassau-Fulda, then passed to [[e:westphalia|Westphalia]] and [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. The poet [[e:hoffmann-von-fallersleben|Hoffmann von Fallersleben]], author of the German national anthem, later worked in its library.

philistine-pentapolis.t: The Philistine Pentapolis, five city-states of the southern Levant coast founded by Aegean newcomers, whose name lives on in Palestine.
philistine-pentapolis.o: Around 1175 BCE [[e:ramesses-iii|Ramesses III]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] repelled the [[e:sea-peoples|Sea Peoples]], including the [[e:philistines|Peleset]]. Groups of these newcomers settled in [[s:gaza|Gaza]], [[s:ashkelon|Ashkelon]], [[s:ashdod|Ashdod]], [[s:ekron|Ekron]] and [[s:gath|Gath]], bringing Aegean-style pottery, cooking habits and pork-eating to the southern coast of [[e:canaan|Canaan]].
philistine-pentapolis.r: Each city was ruled by its own lord, called seren in the [[e:hebrew-bible|Bible]], and they acted together in war. The [[e:philistines|Philistines]] adopted the local Semitic language and gods such as [[e:dagan|Dagon]], and became Israel's main rivals in the stories of [[e:samson|Samson]], [[e:saul|Saul]] and [[e:david|David]].
philistine-pentapolis.e: From the 8th century BCE the cities were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]]. [[e:nebuchadnezzar-ii|Nebuchadnezzar II]] of the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]] destroyed [[s:ashkelon|Ashkelon]] and [[s:ekron|Ekron]] in 604 BCE and deported their people, ending a separate Philistine identity. [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] called the region Palaestina after them.

principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.t: Small Anhalt principality on the Elbe best remembered as the birthplace dynasty of Catherine the Great of Russia.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.o: Rudolf, a son of [[e:joachim-ernest-prince-of-anhalt|Joachim Ernst]], received [[e:zerbst|Zerbst]] in the 1603 partition of [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]]. The town, north of the [[e:elbe|Elbe]], had been a prosperous brewing centre known for its beer, and the line included the lordship of [[e:jever|Jever]] in [[e:frisia|Frisia]], inherited in 1667.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.r: The principality was Lutheran in its later period and modestly governed from a baroque palace in [[e:zerbst|Zerbst]]. Its most famous member was [[e:catherine-the-great|Sophie Auguste Friederike]], daughter of Prince [[e:christian-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst|Christian August]], who married the future [[e:peter-iii-of-russia|Peter III]] and became Empress Catherine II of [[e:russia|Russia]]. Her brother [[e:friedrich-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst|Friedrich August]], the last prince, lived mostly abroad and hired out soldiers to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] during the [[e:american-revolutionary-war|American Revolutionary War]].
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.e: [[e:friedrich-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst|Friedrich August]] died without heirs in 1793. The principality was divided among the other [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] lines, [[e:dessau|Dessau]], [[e:bernburg|Bernburg]] and [[e:kothen|Köthen]], while [[e:jever|Jever]] passed to [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine the Great]] and so to [[e:russia|Russia]].

principality-of-arianiti.t: Lands of the Albanian lord Gjergj Arianiti, who led an early revolt against the Ottomans and became Skanderbeg's ally and father-in-law.
principality-of-arianiti.o: The Arianiti were an old noble family of central [[s:albania|Albania]], holding lands along the [[e:shkumbin|Shkumbin]] valley and around [[e:elbasan|Elbasan]]. In 1432 [[e:gjergj-arianiti|Gjergj Arianiti]], who had been a hostage at the Ottoman court, led a rising against the new Ottoman land registers and defeated several Ottoman armies in the mountains between 1432 and 1436.
principality-of-arianiti.r: Little is known of how the lands were governed: they were a mountain lordship of fortified villages and clan levies rather than a state with fixed institutions, and no clear capital is recorded. Gjergj built ties through marriage, wedding his daughter [[e:donika-kastrioti|Donika]] to [[e:skanderbeg|Skanderbeg]] in 1451, and negotiated with [[e:venice|Venice]], [[e:naples|Naples]] and the [[e:papacy|papacy]].
principality-of-arianiti.e: [[e:gjergj-arianiti|Gjergj Arianiti]] joined the [[s:league-of-lezhe|League of Lezhë]] in 1444, though he later quarrelled with [[e:skanderbeg|Skanderbeg]]. He died in 1462, and the family's lands fell to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in the following years. His descendants, the Arianiti Comneni, settled in [[e:italy|Italy]].

patiala-state.t: The largest of the Sikh Phulkian states of the Punjab, whose maharajas were among the most prominent princes of British India.
patiala-state.o: [[e:ala-singh|Ala Singh]], a Sidhu Jat chief descended from Phul, built up his authority in the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] region of [[e:punjab|Punjab]] from the 1720s and founded the fort of Patiala in 1763. He survived by balancing between the [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] misls and [[e:ahmad-shah-abdali|Ahmad Shah Durrani]], from whom his grandson [[e:amar-singh-of-patiala|Amar Singh]] received the title Raja-i-Rajgan.
patiala-state.r: In 1809 Patiala and the other [[e:cis-sutlej-states|Cis-Sutlej states]] placed themselves under British protection against [[e:ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]]. The rulers supported the British in the Anglo-[[e:sikhism|Sikh]] wars and in 1857, gaining land and honours. [[e:bhupinder-singh-of-patiala|Bhupinder Singh]] (1900–38) was famed for his jewels, cricket patronage and role as Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes. The state had a Sikh ruling house, mixed Sikh, [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Muslim subjects, and a large army.
patiala-state.e: [[e:yadavindra-singh|Yadavindra Singh]] acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947. In 1948 Patiala became the core of the [[s:patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union|Patiala and East Punjab States Union]], with him as [[e:rajpramukh|Rajpramukh]], which was merged into [[e:punjab|Punjab]] in 1956.

prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.t: A Swiss prince-bishopric on Lake Geneva whose bishops ruled Lausanne and its surroundings until Bern conquered Vaud and introduced the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.o: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] of the [[e:aventicum|Avenches]] area moved their seat to [[e:lausanne|Lausanne]] around 600. In 1011 [[e:rudolf-iii-of-burgundy|King Rudolf III of Burgundy]] granted Bishop Henry the county of [[e:vaud|Vaud]], establishing the bishop as a temporal lord. After 1032 the bishops became princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled [[e:lausanne|Lausanne]] and estates such as [[e:lavaux|Lavaux]], famous for vineyards, while the counts of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] dominated the rest of [[e:vaud|Vaud]]. The Gothic cathedral of Lausanne was consecrated in 1275 in the presence of [[e:pope-gregory-x|Pope Gregory X]] and King Rudolf I. The townspeople gradually won rights of self-government.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.e: In 1536 Bern conquered [[e:vaud|Vaud]] from [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], took [[e:lausanne|Lausanne]] and expelled the [[e:bishop|bishop]], introducing the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] after the [[e:lausanne-disputation|Lausanne Disputation]] in which [[e:john-calvin|Calvin]] and [[e:guillaume-farel|Farel]] spoke. Vaud remained Bernese until 1798 and became a Swiss canton in 1803.

prince-abbey-of-kempten.t: Benedictine abbey in the Allgäu whose prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory and rebuilt Kempten in baroque splendour after the Thirty Years War.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.o: The Benedictine abbey of [[e:kempten|Kempten]] was founded in the mid 8th century near the old Roman town of [[e:cambodunum|Cambodunum]] and enjoyed the patronage of [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] wife [[e:hildegard-of-the-vinzgau|Hildegard]]. It gathered estates throughout the [[e:allgau|Allgäu]], and from 1213 its abbots were recognised as princes of the Empire, ruling a secular territory.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.r: The prince-abbots, drawn from the nobility, governed farmers and small towns in the [[e:allgau|Allgäu]] through officials and a strong territorial administration. They clashed constantly with the neighbouring [[s:free-imperial-city-of-kempten|Free Imperial City of Kempten]], which bought its freedom from the abbey in 1525, the year their own peasants rose in the [[e:german-peasants-war|Peasants' War]]. After the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]] Abbot Roman Giel von Gielsberg built the Residenz and the Basilica of St. Lorenz.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and annexed by [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]], which merged the abbey town with the Protestant imperial city into a single [[e:kempten|Kempten]]. The baroque Residenz and basilica survive.

principality-of-jersika.t: An Orthodox principality of the Latgalians on the Daugava, ruled by King Visvaldis until the crusaders of Riga absorbed it.
principality-of-jersika.o: Jersika was a hill fort on the [[e:western-dvina|Daugava]] in eastern [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]] and the centre of a [[e:latgalians|Latgalian]] principality linked to the [[s:principality-of-polotsk|Principality of Polotsk]]. By about 1200 it was ruled by a prince the German sources call [[e:visvaldis|Vissewalde]], known in Latvian as Visvaldis, who was probably of mixed Latgalian and Rus' descent.
principality-of-jersika.r: Jersika controlled trade on the [[e:western-dvina|Daugava]] and ruled over [[e:latgalians|Latgalians]] and [[s:selonians|Selonians]], some of whom were [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Christians with churches. [[e:henry-of-livonia|Henry of Livonia]] calls [[e:visvaldis|Visvaldis]] a king. He allied with the [[e:lithuanians|Lithuanians]] against the German crusaders who had founded Riga.
principality-of-jersika.e: In 1209 [[e:albert-of-riga|Bishop Albert of Riga]] stormed and burned Jersika, captured [[e:visvaldis|Visvaldis's]] wife and forced him to become a [[e:vassal|vassal]], receiving part of his land back as a fief. The rest of his territory passed gradually to Riga and the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], and the principality had disappeared by about 1239.

principality-of-ratzeburg.t: Secularised bishopric east of Lübeck that became a detached province of Mecklenburg-Strelitz for more than two centuries.
principality-of-ratzeburg.o: The Bishopric of [[e:ratzeburg|Ratzeburg]], founded in the 12th century under [[e:henry-the-lion|Henry the Lion]], had become Lutheran in the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 it was secularised and given to the dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] as the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg|Principality of Ratzeburg]], though the town of Ratzeburg itself belonged to Saxe-Lauenburg.
principality-of-ratzeburg.r: The principality was a rural area of villages and farms governed from [[e:schonberg-mecklenburg|Schönberg]]. It had no estates of its own, so its peasants were largely free of the noble domination typical of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]]. Under the Treaty of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] in 1701 it was assigned to the new [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]], from which it was separated by [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]].
principality-of-ratzeburg.e: [[e:ratzeburg|Ratzeburg]] remained part of Mecklenburg-[[e:strelitz|Strelitz]], raised to a grand duchy in 1815, until the monarchy ended in 1918, then belonged to the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]]. Today the area forms part of the district of [[e:nordwestmecklenburg|Nordwestmecklenburg]].

principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.t: The first Serbian state, ruled by the Vlastimirović dynasty in the inland Balkans and converted to Christianity in the 870s.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.o: [[e:serbs|Serbs]] settled in the western [[e:balkans|Balkans]] in the 7th century. [[e:constantine-vii|Constantine VII]] names [[e:viseslav-of-serbia|Višeslav]] as an early prince, usually dated to around 780, but the state becomes clear under [[e:vlastimir|Vlastimir]], who united Serbian tribes in the 830s and repelled an invasion by the Bulgarian khan [[e:presian-i|Presian]] around 839–842.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.r: The ruling prince (knez) shared power with relatives who held districts, and dynastic quarrels were frequent. The principality lay between [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]], often acting as a client of one against the other. Under [[e:mutimir-of-serbia|Mutimir]] the [[e:serbs|Serbs]] adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in the 870s, through Byzantine missions.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.e: [[e:simeon-i-of-bulgaria|Simeon I of Bulgaria]] conquered [[s:serbia|Serbia]] in 924. Prince [[e:caslav-klonimirovic|Časlav]] restored it with Byzantine help from the late 920s, but after his death in the mid-10th century the state fragmented and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] took [[e:ras|Ras]] around 970. Later Serbian states emerged in [[s:duklja|Duklja]] and [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Raška]].

principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.t: Anhalt principality ruled from a castle above the Saale at Bernburg, whose line outlasted every other branch of the 1603 partition except Dessau.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.o: When the [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Principality of Anhalt]] was divided in 1603 among the heirs of [[e:joachim-ernest-prince-of-anhalt|Joachim Ernst]], [[e:christian-i-prince-of-anhalt-bernburg|Christian I]] received [[e:bernburg|Bernburg]]. Christian was a leading Calvinist politician who directed the policy of the [[e:protestant-union|Protestant Union]] and the [[e:elector-palatine|Elector Palatine]] before the defeat at the [[e:battle-of-white-mountain|White Mountain]] in 1620.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.r: The state was small and agrarian, with [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] mining in its [[e:harz|Harz]] exclave around [[e:ballenstedt|Ballenstedt]] and [[e:harzgerode|Harzgerode]]. The ruling line was Calvinist. Branch lines split off, including Anhalt-Bernburg-Schaumburg-Hoym. [[e:bernburg|Bernburg]] was raised to a duchy in 1806, with the court later moving partly to Ballenstedt.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.e: The last duke, [[e:alexander-karl-duke-of-anhalt-bernburg|Alexander Karl]], died childless in 1863, and his lands passed to [[s:principality-of-anhalt-dessau|Anhalt-Dessau]], which thus united all the [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] territories into the [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]]. [[e:bernburg|Bernburg]] remained a district town within Anhalt.

pala-empire.t: The last great Buddhist empire of India, ruling Bengal and Bihar for four centuries and sponsoring the monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.
pala-empire.o: After a century of disorder in [[e:bengal|Bengal]], which later texts call matsyanyaya, the law of the fish, local chiefs chose [[e:gopala-pala-dynasty|Gopala]] as king around 750. His son [[e:dharmapala-pala-emperor|Dharmapala]] expanded the kingdom across [[e:bihar|Bihar]] and installed his own candidate, [[e:chakrayudha|Chakrayudha]] of the [[s:ayudha-dynasty|Ayudha dynasty]], on the throne of [[e:kannauj|Kannauj]].
pala-empire.r: The Palas fought the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]] and the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]] for control of [[e:kannauj|Kannauj]]. They were [[e:mahayana-buddhism|Mahayana]] and [[e:vajrayana|Vajrayana]] Buddhists who also endowed [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]]. [[e:dharmapala-pala-emperor|Dharmapala]] founded [[e:vikramashila|Vikramashila]] and the [[e:somapura-mahavihara|Somapura]] monastery at Paharpur, and [[e:devapala-pala-emperor|Devapala]] supported [[e:nalanda|Nalanda]], which attracted scholars from [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]]. Pala bronze and stone sculpture influenced the art of [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] and [[e:java|Java]], and the monk [[e:atisha|Atisha]], trained in Pala monasteries, helped revive [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] in [[e:tibet|Tibet]].
pala-empire.e: After a decline in the 10th century, [[e:mahipala-i-pala|Mahipala I]] revived the empire, and [[e:ramapala|Ramapala]] suppressed the [[e:varendra-rebellion|Kaivarta revolt]] in north [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. The Palas lost Bengal to the [[s:sena-dynasty|Sena dynasty]] in the 12th century, and the last king, [[e:madanapala|Madanapala]], died around 1161.
